text: Chief complaint should be 1-3 words, patient's own words if possible. Document duration and severity. Example: 'chest pain x 3 days' or 'shortness of breath since this morning.' Avoid abbreviations or medical terminology in the chief complaint.

HPI should follow OPQRST for pain or similar framework for symptoms: Onset (when did it start?), Provocation/Palliation (what makes it better/worse?), Quality (describe in patient's words), Radiation (does it spread?), Severity (1-10 scale), Timing (constant vs intermittent). Include associated symptoms, constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss), and impact on function.

PMH should include: chronic conditions (diabetes, hypertension, CAD, COPD, asthma, CKD, cirrhosis), cancer history with staging and treatment, surgeries with dates, psychiatric history, and substance use (smoking, alcohol, drugs with quantities and duration). Ask specifically about these rather than relying on patient's recall.

PSH should document: type of surgery, date (approximate if unknown), indication, and any complications. Example: 'Appendectomy 2010 for acute appendicitis, no complications.' For recent surgery (<1 year), get operative reports if possible. Note anesthetic type if relevant (general, regional, local).

Document all medications including: prescription drugs (dose, frequency), over-the-counter medications, supplements, and herbal products. Note allergies and adverse reactions separately. Ask about missed doses or non-adherence. Include psychiatric medications, birth control, and 'as needed' medications. Common source of history errors.

Document drug allergies with specific reaction (rash, anaphylaxis, GI upset, etc.). Distinguish true allergies from intolerances. Example: True allergy: 'Penicillin - anaphylaxis (hives, throat closure)' vs Intolerance: 'Amoxicillin - nausea and diarrhea.' Include food and environmental allergies if relevant to presentation.

ROS should be systematic: HEENT (headache, vision changes, hearing, throat pain), Respiratory (cough, SOB, wheezing, hemoptysis), Cardiovascular (chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea, edema), GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain, weight change), GU (dysuria, frequency, hematuria), Neuro (weakness, numbness, vision changes), Psychiatric (mood, suicidal ideation), Musculoskeletal (pain, swelling).

Always record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation (SpO2), and pain level (if applicable). Obtain BP in both arms for new hypertension. Document orthostatic vital signs if syncope or dizziness reported. Note ambient temperature if fever is being assessed. Weight and height for BMI calculation important.

HEENT exam includes: pupils (size, reactivity, equality, accommodation), fundoscopy (optic disc, vessels, hemorrhages, exudates), visual fields, eye movements (CN III, IV, VI), sclera (icteric), conjunctiva (pallor, injection), oral mucosa (hydration), teeth, throat (pharyngeal exudate, erythema), neck veins (JVP), lymph nodes, thyroid.

CV exam: inspection (visible pulsations), palpation (point of maximum impulse location/diameter, thrills), auscultation (rate, rhythm, S1/S2 intensity, murmurs, rubs, S3/S4 gallops), carotid pulse (upstroke, volume, bruits), JVP (height, waveform), peripheral pulses (all 4 extremities), edema (location, severity), skin perfusion (color, temperature, capillary refill).

Pulmonary exam: inspection (work of breathing, retractions, barrel chest), palpation (tactile fremitus, tenderness), percussion (resonance, dullness, hyperresonance), auscultation (breath sounds bilaterally, wheezes, crackles, consolidation, pleural rub). Document location and timing (inspiratory vs expiratory).

Abdominal exam: inspection (distension, scars, visible veins), auscultation (bowel sounds present or absent, bruits), percussion (tympany, dullness), palpation (soft vs firm, tenderness, rebound, guarding, hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, masses, CVA tenderness). Assess for acute abdomen signs.

Neuro exam: mental status (alert, oriented x3), cranial nerves (CN I-XII), motor (strength 0-5 graded, tone, fasciculations), sensory (light touch, vibration, proprioception, pain), reflexes (0-4 graded, symmetry), gait, Romberg, cerebellar signs (ataxia, dysmetria, nystagmus). Document deficits by neuroanatomic location.

Extremity exam: edema (pitting vs non-pitting), cyanosis, clubbing, splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, capillary refill, pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, radial), calf swelling, Homan's sign, varicose veins, skin integrity (wounds, ulcers), hair distribution.

Skin exam: color (pallor, cyanosis, jaundice, erythema), temperature, moisture, turgor (hydration), texture, lesions (macules, papules, vesicles, pustules, plaques, scales, crusts), distribution, blanching (rash blanches with pressure?). Note location precisely. Photography helpful for changing lesions.

Assessment should be problem-focused and organized by problem (not by organ system). Use hierarchical problem list: active problems at top, then resolved/chronic issues. Each problem: differential diagnosis (broad initially, then prioritized), supporting evidence, and investigations needed. Plan addresses each diagnosis/problem sequentially.

Generate broad differential using: organ systems, pathophysiology categories (inflammatory, infectious, neoplastic, metabolic, vascular, trauma), or clinical syndromes. Prioritize by: acuity (life-threatening first), prevalence (common first), and patient risk factors. Use Bayesian thinking: how does test result change pre-test probability? Present differential organized by likelihood.

Write in third-person, objective language. Avoid 'appears', 'seems', 'looks like' - use precise descriptors. Quote patient's words for important symptoms or concerns. Use specific measurements, not vague terms ('6cm mass' not 'large mass'). Avoid unnecessary jargon. Abbreviate standard terms (SOB, fever, CP) but spell out unfamiliar terms first time.

Recognize red flags: signs of sepsis (fever + tachycardia + tachypnea), hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered mental status), severe respiratory distress, chest pain with ECG changes, acute neurologic deficits. In acutely ill patients, stabilize first (airway, breathing, circulation) before detailed history. Document that exam is limited if patient unstable.

text: Dyspnea DDx: Cardiac (MI, heart failure, pulmonary edema, pericarditis, valvular disease), Pulmonary (pneumonia, PE, COPD, asthma, ILD, pneumothorax, pleural effusion), Metabolic (acidosis from DKA, lactic acid), Neuromuscular (Guillain-Barré, myasthenia, ALS), Anemia (if severe, Hgb <7), Anxiety (diagnosis of exclusion). Use vital signs, SpO2, BNP, troponin, chest X-ray, ECG to narrow.

Chest pain DDx: ACS (STEMI, NSTEMI, unstable angina via troponin/ECG), Aortic dissection (sudden, tearing, BP differential), Pulmonary embolism (pleuritic, tachycardia, D-dimer), Pneumonia (fever, productive cough, infiltrate on CXR), Pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, pericardial rub, PR depression on ECG), GERD (burning, worse with food), Costochondritis (reproducible tenderness), Pneumothorax (acute SOB, hyperresonance, no breath sounds). Risk stratify with troponin and ECG immediately.

AMS DDx: Delirium vs dementia vs depression. Delirium = acute confusion with fluctuating course, reversible. Causes: Infection (UTI, pneumonia, meningitis), Metabolic (hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, DKA, hypoglycemia), Medications (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, opioids), Hypoxia, Hypotension, Stroke, Seizure. Dementia = chronic, progressive, baseline cognitive decline. Depression = mood predominant, anhedonia, suicidal ideation.

Fever DDx organized by source: Infectious (viral, bacterial, fungal, parasitic), Inflammatory (vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatologic), Malignancy (lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma), Medications (antibiotics, allopurinol, NSAIDs), Thermoregulatory dysfunction. Use: blood cultures, CBC with differential, CMP, UA/urine culture, CXR, lactate. Duration: acute (<3 weeks) vs chronic (>3 weeks).

Right upper quadrant pain: Biliary (cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis - RUQ pain, + fever, + jaundice = cholangitis), Hepatic (hepatitis, abscess), Pneumonia (right lower lobe), Fitz-Hugh-Curtis (gonococcal perihepatitis). Labs: LFTs, lipase, CBC. Imaging: RUQ ultrasound, CT abdomen. Sign: Murphy's sign suggests cholecystitis.

Left upper quadrant pain: Splenic infarction or rupture (risk: sickle cell, trauma), Gastric/cardiac (angina can present as epigastric/LUQ), Renal (pyelonephritis, nephrolithiasis), Pneumonia (left lower lobe). Less common than RUQ and epigastric pain. Consider splenic rupture in trauma or atrial fibrillation (embolic infarction). CVA tenderness? Consider renal cause.

Epigastric pain: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, acute coronary syndrome (atypical presentation), pancreatitis (epigastric, radiating to back, elevated lipase), gastric malignancy, hepatitis. Key: Does it radiate to back? Suggests pancreatitis. Associated with meal? GERD. Associated with chest symptoms? Consider ACS. Check lipase, troponin, LFTs.

Periumbilical pain: Early appendicitis (before migration to RLQ), small bowel obstruction (crampy, vomiting), gastroenteritis, ischemia (severe pain, minimal findings = 'pain out of proportion'), AAA rupture (severe, hypotensive). Tenderness localizes? Suggests inflammation. Distension? Obstruction. Check lactate for ischemia.

Right lower quadrant pain: Appendicitis (#1, pain starts periumbilical then migrates, fever, rebound tenderness, McBurney's point), IBD (Crohn's disease), ovarian pathology (ovarian torsion, ruptured cyst, PID in females), nephrolithiasis, mesenteric adenitis. McBurney's point: 1/3 distance from ASIS to umbilicus. Imaging: CT abdomen-pelvis.

Left lower quadrant pain: Diverticulitis (older patients, fever, leukocytosis, can perforate), IBD (colitis), ovarian pathology (females), nephrolithiasis, sigmoid volvulus (obstruction, elderly). Diverticulitis risk: low-fiber diet, age >50. CT imaging shows inflamed diverticula. Avoid colonoscopy acutely (perforation risk).

Weakness DDx: Neurologic (stroke, neuropathy, myopathy, myasthenia gravis), Endocrine (hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism), Metabolic (hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia), Hematologic (severe anemia, Hgb <7), Infectious (viral illness), Medications (statins, corticosteroids). Localize: proximal vs distal, upper vs lower extremity, unilateral vs bilateral, acute vs chronic.

Acute SOB (minutes to hours): Pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax, acute coronary syndrome, heart failure exacerbation, COPD exacerbation, anaphylaxis, sepsis, severe anemia. First stabilize: O2, monitor, IV access. Fast assessment: vital signs, cardiac exam (murmur?), lung exam (crackles? wheezes? silent?), extremity exam (calf swelling?), chest X-ray, ECG.

Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT): Gold standard for intervention efficacy. Participants randomly assigned to intervention or control. Minimizes selection bias. Examples: CRASH trial (corticosteroids in head injury), CRASH-2 (tranexamic acid in trauma). Key metrics: RR (relative risk), ARR (absolute risk reduction), NNT (number needed to treat). Interpretation: NNT <10 usually clinically significant.

Cohort studies: Observational, follow groups forward in time. Risk of confounding but useful for natural history. Examples: Framingham Heart Study. Report hazard ratios or relative risks. Lower level of evidence than RCT but can be pragmatic. Prospective cohort stronger than retrospective.

Case-control studies: Look backward. Start with disease outcome, then ascertain exposure. Good for rare diseases. Odds ratio estimated. Risk of recall bias and selection bias. Examples: historical smoking data from interviews. Lower evidence level than RCT/cohort. Cheap and quick to execute.

Cross-sectional studies: Snapshot at one point in time. Prevalence estimated, not incidence. Cannot establish causation. Good for hypothesis generation. Fast and inexpensive. Examples: prevalence surveys. Often used for screening test evaluation.

Systematic review: Structured, reproducible literature search answering specific question. Meta-analysis: statistical combination of multiple studies. Highest evidence level if high-quality studies included. Risk: garbage in = garbage out if included studies biased. PRISMA statement guides conduct.

text: GRADE = Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation. Rates evidence quality (high, moderate, low, very low) and strength of recommendations (strong, weak). Factors: study design, risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, publication bias. Strong recommendation: most informed people agree. Weak: uncertainty, patient values differ.

Sensitivity (TP/[TP+FN]): ability to rule OUT disease (negative test = disease ruled out if high sensitivity). Specificity (TN/[TN+FP]): ability to rule IN disease (positive test = disease present if high specificity). PPV = TP/(TP+FP): probability patient has disease given positive test. NPV = TN/(TN+FN): probability patient disease-free given negative test. Prevalence affects PPV/NPV.

P-value: probability of observing result (or more extreme) if null hypothesis true. P<0.05 traditionally significant. Does NOT mean result is clinically significant or reproducible. 95% CI: range of values that likely contains true population value. Wide CI = imprecision. Narrow CI = precise. CI that crosses 1.0 (RR, OR) = not statistically significant.

NNT = 1/ARR (absolute risk reduction). Represents number of patients needed to treat to prevent one adverse outcome. Example: intervention reduces disease from 20% to 10% = 10% ARR = NNT of 10 (treat 10 patients to prevent 1 outcome). Lower NNT = more effective intervention. Context-dependent: NNT of 2 excellent for serious disease, poor for minor condition.

Risk Ratio (RR) = risk in exposed / risk in unexposed. RR=1 means no difference. RR>1 means increased risk. RR<1 means decreased risk (protective). Odds Ratio (OR) = odds of outcome in exposed / odds in unexposed. OR approximates RR when outcome is rare (<10%). OR overstates effect when outcome common. Interpret: RR 1.5 = 50% increased risk.

NIHSS 1a. Level of consciousness (0-3 points): 0 = alert, 1 = drowsy but arousable, 2 = obtunded/repeated stimulation, 3 = unresponsive. Document what level of stimulation required (verbal vs physical). If intubated or aphasic, document inability to assess.

NIHSS 1b & 1c: Ask patient month and age. 0 = both correct, 1 = one correct, 2 = both wrong. Then ask to open/close eyes and grip both hands. 0 = obeys both, 1 = obeys one, 2 = obeys neither. Aphasic patients: use gestures to demonstrate command. Unresponsive patients: score 3 for both 1b and 1c.

NIHSS 2. Best gaze (0-2): normal = 0, partial gaze palsy = 1, forced deviation = 2. Assess extraocular movements. NIHSS 3. Visual fields (0-3): normal = 0, partial hemianopia = 1, complete hemianopia = 1 side only = 2, bilateral = 3. Test by confrontation or threat if patient cannot cooperate.

metadata.topic: NIHSS Scoring - Gaze and Visual Fields

text: NIHSS 4. Facial palsy (0-3): normal = 0, minor asymmetry = 1, partial paralysis (forehead spared) = 2, complete paralysis one/both sides = 3. Ask patient to show teeth and raise eyebrows. Subtle: ask for maximum effort smile. Score based on asymmetry, not on examiner's opinion of severity. Central vs peripheral can matter clinically.

NIHSS 5. Arm motor - score EACH arm separately (5a left, 5b right). 0-4 scale: 0 = no drift, 1 = drift but doesn't hit surface, 2 = falls before 10 sec, 3 = no effort against gravity, 4 = no movement. Test antigravity: arm outstretched, eyes closed, 10 seconds. Pronation drift (palm down) counts as drift. If can't lift due to pain, score accordingly.

NIHSS 6. Leg motor - score EACH leg separately (6a left, 6b right). 0-4 scale: 0 = no drift, 1 = drift but doesn't hit surface, 2 = falls before 5 sec, 3 = no effort against gravity, 4 = no movement. Test: patient supine, leg elevated to 45 degrees, eyes closed, 5 seconds (note: shorter time than arm). If patient cannot comply (pain, combative), document reason.

NIHSS 7. Limb ataxia (0-2): test FTN (finger-to-nose) and HKS (heel-to-shin) both sides. 0 = no ataxia, 1 = ataxia in one limb, 2 = ataxia in two or more limbs. If weakness present, cannot score ataxia (score 0). FTN: finger extended, patient touches your finger then nose, 5 times. HKS: patient heel slides up opposite shin.

NIHSS 8. Sensory (0-2): test light touch with cotton ball, each side of face, arm, and leg. 0 = normal, 1 = partial loss (patient feels touch but different), 2 = complete loss (does not feel touch) or cannot understand. If patient altered mental status, cannot assess; score based on observation of withdrawal.

NIHSS 9. Best language (0-3): assess with conversation and naming. 0 = normal, 1 = mild aphasia (some word-finding difficulty, but can still communicate), 2 = severe aphasia (mostly unintelligible), 3 = muteness or no meaningful speech. Show objects and ask patient to name (pen, watch, pencil). Dysarthria alone doesn't count as aphasia.

NIHSS 10. Dysarthria (0-2): assess speech clarity when patient reads or repeats words ('mama', 'tip', 'tulip'). 0 = normal, 1 = mild-to-moderate (can be understood), 2 = severe (unintelligible or unable to speak). If patient intubated or ventilator-dependent, score 0 or note 'cannot assess'. Distinguish from aphasia (dysarthria = motor problem, aphasia = language problem).

NIHSS 11. Extinction and inattention (0-2): simultaneous bilateral stimulation (light touch or counting fingers on each side). 0 = normal, 1 = mild (inattention or extinction to one modality), 2 = profound (doesn't recognize one side or in >one modality). Assesses neglect. Can use visual, auditory, tactile stimuli. If altered mental status, cannot assess accurately.

tPA (alteplase) for ischemic stroke: Door-to-needle goal <60 minutes (ideally 30 min). Window: <4.5 hours from symptom onset (FDA approval). Last known well = symptom onset time. CT head required to rule out hemorrhage before tPA. Dose: 0.9 mg/kg (max 90 mg), 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min. Concurrent antiplatelet agents generally avoided first 24 hrs.

Absolute contraindications to tPA: active intracranial hemorrhage, recent (within 3 months) intracranial surgery/head trauma, history of intracranial hemorrhage, suspected aortic dissection, uncontrolled hypertension (systolic >185 mmHg or diastolic >110 mmHg), INR >1.7 on warfarin, prothrombin time >15 sec, thrombocytopenia (<100,000), recent GI/urinary bleed. Relative: seizure, diabetic retinopathy, major surgery <3 months.

Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) for large vessel occlusion (LVO): can extend window to 24 hours in selected patients with imaging showing viable tissue (DAWN, DEFUSE 3 trials). Large artery occlusion detected on CTA (ICA, M1, basilar). MT superior to tPA alone for LVO in <24hr window. Coordination with interventional radiology critical. Door-to-puncture time important.

Non-contrast CT head: rule out hemorrhage before tPA (sensitivity 95%+). CTA (computed tomography angiography): detect large vessel occlusion, assess collateral flow. CTP (perfusion): shows perfusion mismatch (ischemic core vs penumbra). MRI DWI/PWI: gold standard for acute ischemia (shows infarct within minutes). Vessel imaging: carotid imaging (CTA, ultrasound, MRA) for stroke etiology.

After tPA: no anticoagulation or antiplatelet for 24 hours. Neuro checks every 15 min x 2 hours, then 30 min x 6 hours, then hourly x 16 hours. ICU admission typical. Repeat CT 24 hours after tPA to rule out hemorrhagic transformation (10-15% of tPA cases; usually asymptomatic). Monitor for symptomatic ICH (large volume hemorrhage). Hypertension management: permissive (SBP <180-230) first 24h.

Spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) presents with severe headache, focal neurologic deficits, often with altered consciousness. Non-contrast CT: shows blood (white). Causes: hypertension (basal ganglia, thalamus), amyloid angiopathy (lobar), vascular malformation (AVM, cavernoma), anticoagulation, sympathomimetics (cocaine), reversible cerebral vasoconstriction (RCVS), subarachnoid hemorrhage. Prognosis: poor (30-day mortality 40-50%).

ICH management: admit to ICU, frequent neuro checks, reverse anticoagulation if present. SBP goal usually 140-160 (avoid excessive lowering = ischemia). Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, fever, hyperglycemia. DVT prophylaxis delayed if ICH active. Surgical consultation if mass effect, lobar hemorrhage with herniation risk, or posterior fossa hemorrhage. Medication: labetalol, nicardipine for HTN; mannitol or hypertonic saline for increased ICP.

After stroke: antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, clopidogrel, aspirin+dipyridamole). Statin (high-intensity). Blood pressure control (target SBP <130 in most). Glucose control (target 140-180 in acute). Lipids, smoking cessation, exercise, diet. Atrial fibrillation screening: ECG, consider Holter/event monitor. Carotid disease: imaging if TIA/stroke in carotid distribution. Anticoagulation if cardioembolic source (e.g., AFib).

Status epilepticus = continuous seizures >5 minutes OR recurrent seizures without return to baseline consciousness between events. Medical emergency. Mortality 10-15% if untreated. Convulsive status (generalized tonic-clonic) vs non-convulsive (focal, absence, myoclonic status). Non-convulsive status: subtle or no motor activity but abnormal EEG and altered mental status. Treatment principles same regardless of type.

Stabilize: ABCs first. Protect airway, supplemental O2, IV access. Place patient in recovery position if not already. Stop seizure activity. Get blood glucose immediately (hypoglycemia mimics seizure). Check vital signs, temp. Obtain brief collateral history: prior seizures? Medications? Compliance? Trauma? Fever? Recent infections? Exposures? Document seizure type/duration if witnessed.

First-line: IV lorazepam 4 mg push, repeat q2-5min up to 8 mg total (fastest onset). OR IM midazolam 10 mg (if no IV access, faster than lorazepam). OR rectal diazepam 20 mg. Benzodiazepine goal: stop seizure within 3-5 minutes. Concurrent loading of second-line agent (fosphenytoin or levetiracetam). Continue if seizure persists.

Second-line (administer concurrently with benzos): Fosphenytoin 15-20 PE/kg IV (faster, safer than phenytoin - no cardiac toxicity, can infuse at any rate). OR Levetiracetam 500-2000 mg IV (no drug interactions, no loading). Fosphenytoin traditional choice, levetiracetam gaining favor (fewer drug interactions, no cardiac concerns). If seizure continues after first AND second agent: prepare for intubation, third-line agent.

Third-line (refractory status): propofol (0.5-1 mg/kg IV load, then 1-3 mg/kg/hr infusion) - requires intubation/ICU, can cause myocardial depression. OR pentobarbital (5-15 mg/kg load over 1 hour, then 0.5-1 mg/kg/hr). OR continuous midazolam infusion after loading. These agents require ICU-level monitoring, propofol requires central line often. Goal: stop electrical activity on EEG.

First unprovoked seizure: neuroimaging (MRI brain preferred, or CT if urgent), EEG (ideally during seizure, if possible record video). Blood work: glucose, electrolytes, Ca, Mg, CBC, LFTs, drug screen, anticonvulsant levels if on meds. Lumbar puncture if fever or meningitis concern. Do NOT start antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) after single unprovoked seizure (high recurrence risk ~40%, but many patients never have second seizure). Refer to neurology.

Seizure etiologies: idiopathic/genetic, structural (tumor, stroke, AVM, traumatic brain injury, scar), metabolic (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, uremia), infectious (meningitis, encephalitis, cysticercosis), alcohol withdrawal, medications, sleep deprivation, fever (febrile seizures in children). First seizure: broad workup. Recurrent seizures: establish etiology, start AEDs.

Maintenance AEDs (for recurrent seizures): Phenytoin (Dilantin) - narrow therapeutic index, many drug interactions. Levetiracetam (Keppra) - well-tolerated, no interactions, no TDM needed. Valproic acid (Depakote) - broad spectrum, requires TDM, risk of hepatotoxicity and pancreatitis. Lamotrigine (Lamictal) - slow titration (rash risk), effective. Lacosamide (Vimpat) - newer, cardiac concerns. Choice depends on seizure type, comorbidities, interactions.

Provoked seizure: identifiable trigger (alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycemia, infection, medication, sleep deprivation, trauma). Treat underlying cause, short-term seizure coverage often sufficient. No long-term AED required if etiology reversed. Unprovoked seizure: no clear trigger, inherent brain tendency to seize. Requires evaluation for underlying structural/metabolic cause and long-term AED therapy. Risk of recurrence higher with unprovoked seizures.

Pregnancy and seizures: most AEDs have some teratogenic risk, but untreated seizures also risk fetus (maternal injury, status, placental abruption). Counsel preconception if possible. First trimester highest risk. Folic acid supplementation standard (5mg daily). Phenytoin and valproic acid higher teratogenic risk. Levetiracetam favorable safety profile. Continue AED during pregnancy (seizure control > teratogenic risk). Special monitoring: drug levels change with pregnancy, renal clearance increases.

Bacterial meningitis: Streptococcus pneumoniae (#1 in adults), Neisseria meningitidis (serogroup B most common, spreadable = isolation), Listeria monocytogenes (age >50, immunocompromised). Viral meningitis: enterovirus most common. Risk factors: asplenia, CSF leak, immunocompromise, crowded living, age extremes. Incidence US ~1 per 100,000. Mortality bacterial 15-20% even with treatment.

Classic triad (only ~50% present): fever, headache, neck stiffness. Altered mental status (confusion, lethargy), photophobia, kernig sign (knee flexion pain with hip/knee extended), brudzinski sign (neck flexion causes hip/knee flexion). Rash: petechial (especially meningococcemia), maculopapular, purpuric. Rapid progression possible (fulminant meningococcemia). Young children: may lack classic signs, present with irritability, lethargy only. High suspicion key.

Lumbar puncture findings: Bacterial - glucose <40 mg/dL (or <45% of serum), protein 100-500 (often >500), WBC 1000-10000 (PMN predominant, 85%+), Gram stain positive 50-80%, culture positive 70-80%. Viral - glucose normal/mildly low, protein 50-200, WBC 100-1000 (lymphocyte predominant after first 24h), culture negative. Fungal - glucose <40, protein very high 200-500+, lymphocytic, India ink/cryptococcal antigen positive.

Procalcitonin: elevated in bacterial meningitis, normal in viral (useful rapid test for bacterial vs viral discrimination). Blood cultures: positive in 50-70% bacterial cases; draw before antibiotics. CBC: elevated WBC with left shift in bacterial. CMP: check glucose (for CSF/serum glucose ratio), renal function (dosing adjustment needed). Consider PCR panels for meningitis (multiplex PCR faster than culture).

CT head: perform BEFORE LP if papilledema, focal deficits, immunocompromised (risk of herniation from LP). If normal, can proceed with LP. MRI: more sensitive for subdural empyema, ventriculitis. CXR: assess for pneumonia (common source). Imaging findings: basilar enhancement (TB, fungal), ventricular enlargement, subdural collections.

Empiric antibiotics (BEFORE culture results): Age 18-50 healthy: Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h + Vancomycin 15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h. Age >50 or immunocompromised: ADD Ampicillin 2g IV q4h (covers Listeria - cephalosporins don't). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV q6h x 4 days (started with FIRST antibiotic dose = reduces mortality). Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for LP if meningitis suspected. Remove when culture returns (tailor based on organism).

Empiric neonatal antibiotics: Ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV q12h (or cefotaxime 50 mg/kg IV q8h) + Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV q6h. Dexamethasone controversial in neonates (may reduce inflammation too much). Causes: Group B Streptococcus (penicillin/cephalosporin-susceptible), E. coli (K1 antigen), Listeria. Dosing differs from older children/adults. Close follow-up neurology important (hearing loss from meningitis 20-30%).

Supportive: fluid management (avoid hyponatremia from SIADH), seizure prophylaxis (short-term benzodiazepine if seizure risk), antipyretics. Complications: subdural empyema, ventriculitis, hydrocephalus (may need external ventricular drain), hearing loss (sensorineural, permanent), neurologic sequelae (learning disability, developmental delay, epilepsy). 10-30% survivors have long-term neuro deficit. Outcome better with early antibiotics and steroids.

Droplet precautions for suspected/confirmed meningitis: N95 mask, isolation room preferred, contact precautions for secretions. Duration: until 24 hours after first effective antibiotic dose AND clinical improvement. Meningococcal meningitis particularly contagious = notify public health, consider chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (e.g., household members, healthcare workers with mouth-to-mouth contact). Prophylaxis: rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone IM.

Mortality bacterial meningitis: 15-20% despite antibiotics, higher in elderly/immunocompromised. Meningococcal fulminant: can be 40-50%. Viral meningitis: <1% mortality (generally self-limited). Morbidity: hearing loss (30%), developmental delay (children), neurologic sequelae (learning disability, epilepsy), subdural empyema. Early recognition and antibiotics + dexamethasone critical for best outcomes. Vaccination (pneumococcal, meningococcal) prevents disease.

STEMI = ST-elevation myocardial infarction. ECG diagnostic criteria: ≥1mm ST elevation in contiguous leads (≥2mm in precordial leads V1-V3 acceptable). New LBBB with appropriate concordance also counts as STEMI equivalent. Troponin elevation confirms myocardial necrosis. Requires reperfusion therapy (PCI or fibrinolysis) within 120 minutes to salvage myocardium. Window critical: every minute of delay increases mortality.

NSTEMI = no ST elevation but troponin elevated (high-sensitivity troponin within hours; conventional troponin 3-6 hours). Unstable angina = chest pain/ACS symptoms but normal troponin (negative predictive value >99% with high-sensitivity troponin at 0 and 2 hours). Both have similar pathophysiology (plaque rupture, partial thrombosis) but better prognosis than STEMI. Risk stratification (TIMI, GRACE) guides medical therapy, catheterization timing, antiplatelet intensity.

Conventional troponin: rises 3-6 hours post-MI, peaks 24-48 hours, normalizes 7-14 days. High-sensitivity troponin: rises within 1-3 hours, higher sensitivity (>99%). Serial troponins improve diagnostic accuracy. Serial change more valuable than single value: delta rise/fall algorithm (>20% relative change suggests acute MI). Elevated troponin not pathognomonic: occurs in sepsis, PE, heart failure, kidney disease, atrial fibrillation, endocarditis. Integration with clinical/ECG findings critical.

Atypical ACS presentations increase with: female sex, age >75, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, heart failure. Presentations: dyspnea without chest pain (silent MI in elderly/diabetics), epigastric discomfort (confused with GERD), jaw/arm/back pain, syncope, altered mental status, acute decompensated heart failure. Women often have chest discomfort more atypical (nausea, fatigue, shortness of breath). Diabetics have high prevalence of silent MI (autonomic neuropathy). High suspicion needed; obtain ECG/troponin liberally.

ACS differentials: aortic dissection (sudden, tearing, hypotension, pulse differentials), PE (pleuritic, tachycardia, risk factors), pneumonia (fever, infiltrate, productive cough), pericarditis (pleuritic, positional, pericardial rub, PR depression), GERD (relation to meals, relief with antacids), musculoskeletal pain (reproducible, positional), anxiety (normal ECG/troponin). ECG + troponin + chest X-ray narrow differential. Troponin negative + normal ECG = low risk for ACS (negative predictive value >99%).

metadata.topic: Differential Diagnosis of Chest Pain - ACS vs Non-ACS

text: TIMI Risk Score (0-7 points): age ≥65 (1), ≥3 CAD risk factors (1), prior CAD (1), aspirin use in past 7 days (1), severe angina ≥2 episodes in 24h (1), ST changes (1), elevated troponin (1). Score 0-1: low risk, 2: intermediate, 3-4: high, 5-7: very high risk. Predicts 14-day mortality/MI/revascularization. Guides antiplatelet intensity (P2Y12 inhibitor dose), timing of catheterization (within 24h for high risk, can delay low risk).

GRACE Score (Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events): incorporates age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip class, ST deviation, troponin elevation, in-hospital mortality/6-month mortality. More comprehensive than TIMI. Score <100: low risk. 100-140: intermediate. >140: high risk. Predicts longer-term outcomes. Used to risk-stratify for invasive vs conservative strategy. Online calculator available. Particularly useful when multiple risk factors present or uncertainty about stratification.

ACS patient initial management: oxygen if SpO2 <90%, IV access (large bore), continuous cardiac monitoring, ECG within 10 minutes, troponin/CBC/CMP/coagulation studies, chest X-ray, pain control (morphine 2-4mg IV, repeat q5-15min), urgent cardiology consultation. Nitrates if hypertensive/pulmonary edema (caution if RV infarction). Beta-blocker if tachycardia/hypertension (avoid if AV block/shock). ACE inhibitor early if tolerating. Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) immediately for all ACS.

metadata.topic: ACS - Acute Presentation and Initial Stabilization

text: Left anterior descending (LAD) STEMI: ST elevation in V1-V4, I, aVL. Extensive anterior MI if involves V1-V4, I, aVL (high mortality). Diagonal branch involvement: ST elevation V1-V4, aVL, but not II, III, aVF. Associated: high-degree AV block (LAD septal perforator), Mobitz II, complete heart block, anterior wall rupture (mechanical complications), cardiogenic shock common. Loss of septal Q waves suggests septal necrosis.

Right coronary artery (RCA) STEMI: ST elevation II, III, aVF (inferior wall). Right ventricular involvement: ST elevation V4R (right-sided ECG lead). Associated: bradycardia (sinus node involvement), high-degree AV block (proximal RCA at nodal artery), hypotension (RV infarction), usually better prognosis than LAD. KEY: RV infarction contraindication = nitrates/IV morphine (preload-dependent; use caution). Fluid bolus may help restore blood pressure.

Left circumflex (LCx) STEMI: ST elevation I, aVL, sometimes V5-V6. Posterior wall MI: ST depression V1-V3 (reciprocal changes) with ST elevation in posterior leads (V7-V9 on right side, or use posterior precordial leads). Posterior MI can be subtle; evaluate posterior leads if inferior/posterior symptoms. LCx occlusion at distal margin: mild involvement; proximal: extends to RV. Prognosis intermediate between LAD and RCA.

metadata.topic: ECG Localization - Left Circumflex Territory and Posterior MI

text: RV infarction: occurs in ~50% of inferior wall MIs. ST elevation V4R (right-sided ECG) diagnostic. Presentation: hypotension disproportionate to MI size, elevated JVP, clear lung fields (unlike LV failure). Management: fluid bolus (crystalloid) cautiously to restore RV filling (critical for RV output). AVOID nitrates and morphine (decrease preload, worsen shock). AVOID beta-blockers if bradycardic (AV block already present). Maintain HR 60-80 and BP >90. RV infarction usually recovers within days.

metadata.topic: Right Ventricular Infarction - Recognition and Management

text: Primary PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention) preferred over fibrinolysis if available within 120 minutes door-to-balloon time. PCI advantages: higher TIMI 3 flow, lower reocclusion, better mortality (7-8% vs 9-10% for fibrinolysis). Fibrinolysis: faster door-to-needle (30 min), useful if PCI delay >120 min, patient transfer >90 min, or PCI unavailable. Contraindications to fibrinolysis: active bleeding, prior ICH, recent surgery, aortic dissection. Early transfer for PCI reasonable if <3 hours from symptom onset even if fibrinolysis initiated.

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid): irreversible COX inhibition, platelet aggregation inhibition. Loading dose: 325-500mg PO (chewed for faster absorption) or 250-500mg IV. Maintenance: 81-325mg daily (higher doses increase GI bleed risk). Onset: 15-30 minutes. Side effects: GI bleed (especially with concurrent NSAID/corticosteroids), bleeding complications, drug allergy (rash, anaphylaxis). Hold for ≥5 days before elective surgery if possible (platelet dysfunction persists). Use in all ACS unless contraindicated (allergy, active bleeding).

metadata.topic: Aspirin in ACS - Dosing and Mechanism

text: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) = aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor. Clopidogrel (Plavix): 600mg loading (or 300mg), 75mg daily. Slower onset, prodrug requiring CYP3A4 metabolism. Ticagrelor (Brilinta): 180mg loading, 60mg BID. Faster onset, stronger P2Y12 binding, reversible. Prasugrel (Effient): 60mg loading (5mg if <60kg/age >75), 5mg daily. Fastest onset, strongest platelet inhibition, higher bleeding risk. Ticagrelor preferred over clopidogrel in STEMI (faster). Prasugrel reserved for angiography-proven CAD. All require DDP-DES or BMS placement for DAPT duration.

DAPT duration: typically 12 months for ACS (STEMI or NSTEMI). Bare-metal stents (BMS): minimum 1 month, then aspirin monotherapy. Drug-eluting stents (DES): minimum 3-6 months, typically extend to 12 months for ACS. Shorter duration (3-6 months): consider if high bleeding risk (age, renal disease, anemia, oral anticoagulant needed). Longer duration (>12 months): consider if low bleeding risk, high thrombotic risk (diabetes, complex anatomy, prior stent thrombosis). Aspirin monotherapy indefinitely post-DAPT.

metadata.topic: DAPT Duration - Balancing Stent Thrombosis vs Bleeding

text: Beta-blockers reduce mortality post-MI (15-20% relative risk reduction). Acute use: reduce cardiac work, heart rate, blood pressure. IV metoprolol 25-50mg, then PO maintenance (target HR 50-60). Esmolol for temporary control. Cautions: avoid if bradycardia <50, hypotension, AV block, decompensated heart failure, RV infarction (loss of RV chronotropic support). Continue long-term post-MI unless contraindicated. Cardioselective agents (metoprolol, atenolol) preferred over non-selective (propranolol).

metadata.topic: Beta-Blockers in ACS - Acute and Long-term Use

text: ACE inhibitors (lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril): reduce LV remodeling post-MI, lower mortality 20%, particularly if anterior MI or reduced EF (<40%). Start within 24-48 hours (after acute stabilization, BP adequate). Dose: lisinopril 5mg daily, titrate to 10-40mg daily. Cautions: hyperkalemia risk (especially if renal disease), hypotension, cough (15-20%). Check renal function, potassium before/after initiation. Continue indefinitely unless contraindicated. ARBs (losartan) alternative if ACE-I intolerant (cough).

metadata.topic: ACE Inhibitors in ACS - Indication and Timing

text: High-intensity statins reduce LDL, reduce cardiovascular events/mortality. Acute MI: initiate high-dose statin immediately (atorvastatin 80mg daily or rosuvastatin 40mg daily) regardless of baseline LDL. Continue indefinitely. LDL target: <70 mg/dL (or <55 if very high risk). Side effects: myalgia (rare but significant statin intolerance), elevated transaminases (monitor baseline), myositis/rhabdomyolysis (rare), drug interactions (avoid certain statins with CYP3A4 inhibitors). Check lipid panel, CK baseline. Benefits far outweigh risks in ACS.

Nitrates: reduce preload, afterload, coronary vasodilation (improves collateral blood flow). Acute use: SL nitroglycerin 0.3-0.6mg q5 minutes x 3 doses (within 10 minutes of symptom onset). IV nitroglycerin for ongoing chest pain or hypertension/pulmonary edema. Cautions: avoid if hypotensive (SBP <90), RV infarction (preload-dependent), concurrent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil = profound hypotension). Tolerance develops with continuous use; use dosing intervals to prevent. Long-term nitrate use limited in ACS (no mortality benefit).

metadata.topic: Nitroglycerin in ACS - Uses and Precautions

text: Morphine: potent opioid analgesia, anxiolysis, reduces preload (mild), decreases adrenergic tone. Dosing: 2-4mg IV, repeat q5-15 min until pain controlled. Side effects: respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia (via vagal effect), histamine release (caution in aspiration risk). Caution: avoid in inferior MI with RV involvement (preload-dependent) or cardiogenic shock. Modern trend: less reliance on morphine (increases heart rate via compensation, may worsen ischemia); use cautiously, preferring beta-blockers/nitrates. Pain relief reduces sympathetic stress response.

metadata.topic: Morphine in ACS - Analgesia and Hemodynamic Effects

text: Anticoagulation during ACS/PCI: unfractionated heparin (UFH) IV bolus 50-100 units/kg, then continuous infusion (goal aPTT 50-70 seconds). LMWH (enoxaparin) 1mg/kg IV bolus for PCI. UFH preferred if planned urgent angiography (reversible by protamine, shorter half-life). LMWH comparable efficacy, more predictable, used if conservative strategy. Target: prevent stent thrombosis, recurrent ACS. Duration: typically 24-48 hours for STEMI, shorter for stable NSTEMI. Check platelets for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT, rare but serious).

metadata.topic: Anticoagulation in ACS - Unfractionated Heparin and LMWH

text: GP IIb/IIIa inhibitors (abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban): potent antiplatelet agents, block final common pathway of platelet aggregation. Use in PCI (especially STEMI, thrombotic lesions): given IV bolus, then infusion. Abciximab 0.25mg/kg bolus, then 0.125 mcg/kg/min infusion. Reduces ischemic complications during PCI, improves outcomes. Cautions: bleeding risk (especially with dual antiplatelet therapy + anticoagulation), thrombocytopenia (check platelets), requires careful coordination with other antiplatelet agents. Used less frequently now (dual antiplatelet therapy + newer P2Y12 inhibitors effective).

metadata.topic: Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa Inhibitors - Use in PCI

text: Calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil, nifedipine): generally avoided in acute STEMI/NSTEMI due to lack of mortality benefit vs beta-blockers. Verapamil/diltiazem non-dihydropyridines can worsen heart failure if EF reduced. Nifedipine (dihydropyridine) increases tachycardia/reflex activation, counterproductive. Limited role: rate control in NSTEMI if beta-blocker contraindicated/intolerant, or for hypertension control. No indication for routine use in ACS. Long-acting nifedipine acceptable for chronic CAD management post-MI.

metadata.topic: Calcium Channel Blockers in ACS - Limited Role

text: Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone, eplerenone): reduce mortality in post-MI heart failure with reduced EF (EF <40%). Typical: eplerenone 25mg daily, titrate to 50mg daily (or spironolactone 12.5-25mg daily). Mechanism: blocks aldosterone-mediated fibrosis, improves ventricular remodeling. Side effect: hyperkalemia risk (check baseline K+, renal function; recheck at 3-7 days, then periodically). Indication: documented reduced EF post-MI, not just during acute event. Continue indefinitely if tolerated.

metadata.topic: Aldosterone Antagonists in ACS with Reduced EF

text: Cardiogenic shock: hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) + evidence of hypoperfusion (altered mental status, cool extremities, oliguria, lactate >2) due to left ventricular dysfunction post-MI. Incidence 5-8% of acute MI, mortality 50-80%. Causes: extensive LV infarction (>40% LV mass), mechanical complications (MR, VSD, rupture), RV infarction, arrhythmias. Management: revascularization (emergency PCI, IABP, mechanical support), inotropes/vasopressors (dobutamine, milrinone, norepinephrine), diuretics (cautiously), monitor closely in ICU.

metadata.topic: Cardiogenic Shock Post-MI - Pathophysiology and Management

text: Acute mitral regurgitation post-MI: due to papillary muscle rupture (partial or complete) in posteromedial infarction (RCA territory 70%, LCx 20%). Presents with acute dyspnea, hypoxia, new holosystolic murmur, pulmonary edema. Diagnosis: echocardiography (color Doppler shows regurgitant jet). Partial rupture: medical management (vasodilators, inotropes) with urgent surgery. Complete rupture: cardiogenic shock, requires emergency mitral valve repair/replacement. Mortality high (mortality 50-70% if unrepaired).

VSD post-MI: ventricular septal rupture within days of MI (usually anterior MI with LAD occlusion). Presents with new holosystolic murmur, abrupt hypotension, pulmonary edema, right-to-left shunt (hypoxia). Diagnosis: echocardiography with color Doppler (shunt flow visible), cardiac catheterization (O2 saturation step-up from RV to PA). Hemodynamically significant VSD requires urgent surgical repair (mortality 25-40% if surgery, >90% if medical management alone). IABP, vasodilators, inotropes temporary bridge to surgery.

metadata.topic: Mechanical Complications - Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD) Post-MI

text: Left ventricular free wall rupture: catastrophic complication (1-3% of MIs), usually 3-7 days post-MI, mortality >90%. Risk factors: first MI, anterior location, older age, female, delayed reperfusion, excessive anticoagulation. Presentation: sudden severe chest pain, hemodynamic collapse, tamponade physiology, pulseless electrical activity. Diagnosis: echo with pericardial fluid/hemopericardium, or clinical presentation. Management: emergency pericardiocentesis (temporary), then emergency surgery (repair patch, support). Subacute presentation (pseudoaneurysm) may allow delayed surgery.

Bradycardia/heart block post-MI: caused by ischemia of conducting tissue. Inferior MI (RCA): sinus bradycardia, AV blocks (Mobitz I/II, complete), usually transient. Anterior MI (LAD): His bundle ischemia, Mobitz II/complete block with wide QRS escape, poor prognosis. Management: atropine 0.5-1mg IV for symptomatic bradycardia (inferior MI responsive), temporary pacing if hemodynamic compromise, permanent pacing if persistent high-degree block (anterior MI). Avoid beta-blockers if bradycardia. Monitor telemetry closely.

metadata.topic: Post-Infarction Arrhythmias - Bradycardia and Conduction Blocks

text: Ventricular fibrillation (VF): primary (within 48 hours of MI onset) or secondary (due to cardiogenic shock, pump failure). Primary VF: immediate defibrillation, ACLS protocol. Mortality 3-5% if treated promptly, >90% if delayed. Ventricular tachycardia (VT): can be sustained or non-sustained. Treat if hemodynamically unstable: immediate defibrillation if pulseless, amiodarone IV if hemodynamic tolerance. Beta-blockers reduce VT/VF risk. Long-term: ICD placement if EF <35 post-MI (ischemic cardiomyopathy).

metadata.topic: Post-Infarction Arrhythmias - Ventricular Fibrillation and Tachycardia

text: Post-MI LV remodeling: acute dilation (within hours), then eccentric hypertrophy (days to weeks) if large MI. Results in reduced EF, heart failure symptoms. Prevention/slowing: early reperfusion (limits infarct size), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, aldosterone antagonists, cardiac rehabilitation. LV thrombus risk: increased if anterior MI, large infarct, low EF, akinetic/dyskinetic segment. Prophylaxis: warfarin or DOAC if thrombus documented (goal INR 2-3), or if EF <30 + anterior MI + anterior akinesis (controversial). Echocardiography at discharge to assess EF, complications.

metadata.topic: Left Ventricular Remodeling and Heart Failure Post-MI

text: Post-MI pericarditis: inflammation from transmural infarction/pericardial irritation. Early (within 24-72 hours): pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub, may mimic recurrent ischemia. Late (Dressler's syndrome, weeks-months post-MI): fever, pleurisy, pericarditis, pericardial effusion, sometimes with tamponade. Management: NSAIDs (aspirin, indomethacin), colchicine. Avoid in presence of reduced EF or fluid restriction needed. Steroids reserved for refractory cases. Distinguish from recurrent ischemia/infarction (troponin elevation more marked in infarction).

RV infarction complications: hypotension (loss of RV contractility), bradycardia/AV blocks (nodal ischemia), atrial fibrillation (RA ischemia). Recurrent ischemia: RV infarction patients high risk; reperfusion critical. Long-term: most recover within days to weeks; persistent RV dysfunction rare. Tricuspid regurgitation may develop (secondary to RV dilatation). RV function assessed by echo; improvement typically occurs. Low mortality if uncomplicated by LV involvement or hemodynamic decompensation.

metadata.topic: Right Ventricular Infarction - Complications and Long-term Sequelae

text: Myocardial rupture mechanisms differ by location: (1) Papillary muscle: MR symptom, preserved systolic function initially; (2) Ventricular septum: VSD physiology, step-up in saturation; (3) Free wall: tamponade, shock, pulseless arrest. All occur 3-7 days post-MI typically. Risk: older age, first MI, female, lack of collaterals, hypertension in acute phase, excess anticoagulation. Prevention: early reperfusion, avoid excessive anticoagulation, control BP. Prognosis: free wall worst, VSD intermediate, MR variable depending on extent.

metadata.topic: Myocardial Rupture Variants - Papillary Muscle vs Septum vs Wall

text: Post-infarction angina: ischemia in different coronary territory from initial MI (not same vessel). Risk: incomplete revascularization, progression of CAD, stent restenosis. Presents with chest pain similar to initial MI. Troponin may be elevated from original MI (doesn't reset for 7-14 days). Serial troponins/ECG changes help distinguish (new elevation = reinfarction). Management: urgent catheterization/PCI if recurrent angina. Preventive: optimal medical therapy (dual antiplatelet, beta-blockers, ACE-I, statins, revascularization), smoking cessation, risk factor control.

metadata.topic: Recurrent Angina Post-MI - Postinfarction Angina vs Reinfarction

text: Discharge medications (essential): dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor), beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, high-intensity statin, consider aldosterone antagonist if EF <40%. Dosing optimization: beta-blocker target HR 50-60, SBP 100-120; ACE-I titrate to maximum tolerated. Discharge checklist: smoking cessation counseling, cardiac rehabilitation referral, follow-up cardiology appointment, PCI documentation, EF assessment (echo), ICD consideration if EF <35 post-stabilization (30 days post-MI).

metadata.topic: Post-MI Discharge Planning and Medication Optimization

text: Cardiac rehabilitation: supervised exercise training, education on risk factor modification, psychosocial support. Benefits: improved functional capacity, reduced mortality (20-30% RRR), improved quality of life. Phases: Phase I (acute hospitalization), Phase II (3-6 weeks post-discharge, supervised supervised outpatient), Phase III (long-term home-based). Components: aerobic exercise (target 150 min/week moderate intensity), dietary counseling (heart-healthy diet, DASH), smoking cessation, stress management, medication education. Refer all post-MI patients; contraindications rare (hemodynamic instability, ongoing ischemia).

Post-MI secondary prevention: (1) Smoking cessation: counseling + pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion) reduces cardiac events 50%+. (2) Lipid targets: LDL <70, or <55 if very high risk; use high-intensity statins, consider ezetimibe/PCSK9 inhibitors if LDL not at goal. (3) Blood pressure: target <130/80 (higher targets if dialysis/advanced CKD). (4) Diabetes: tight glucose control (target HbA1c 7% non-fragile), GLP-1 agonist/SGLT2i for cardioprotection. (5) Physical activity: 150 min/week moderate intensity, resistance training 2x/week.

metadata.topic: Risk Factor Modification - Smoking, Lipids, Blood Pressure

text: Anticoagulation post-PCI: dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor) standard. Additional anticoagulation (UFH/LMWH/fondaparinux) during acute phase only (typically 24-48 hours). Long-term oral anticoagulation (warfarin/DOAC) indicated if: (1) LV thrombus, (2) atrial fibrillation, (3) hypercoagulable state. Balance between thrombotic (stent thrombosis, recurrent MI) and bleeding risks. Triple therapy (aspirin + P2Y12 + anticoagulation) increases bleeding risk significantly; requires careful patient selection. Proton pump inhibitor for GI bleed prophylaxis if triple therapy.

metadata.topic: Anticoagulation Strategy Post-PCI - DAPT vs Anticoagulation

text: ICD indication: reduced EF ≤35% at >40 days post-MI (allow time for recovery). Placement: single-chamber ICD if sinus rhythm no indication for pacing, dual-chamber if bradycardia/need for rate-responsive pacing, biventricular ICD if QRS >120ms + symptomatic heart failure (CRT-D). Wearable defibrillator temporary option if EF 25-35% and uncertain recovery. Prevents sudden cardiac death, improves survival in ischemic cardiomyopathy. Refer to EP for evaluation if EF <35% at 6 weeks.

Stress testing (exercise treadmill, stress echo, nuclear) at 3-6 weeks post-MI to assess for inducible ischemia (risk stratification). Indications: intermediate EF, symptoms suggesting ongoing ischemia, equivocal revascularization. Viability testing (stress echo, nuclear imaging, late-gadolinium enhancement MRI) identifies potentially salvageable myocardium (>50% wall thickness) in akinetic/dyskinetic segments. Viability presence suggests consideration for revascularization in heart failure (ISCHEMIA-CHF, STICH trials showed modest benefit). Absence of viability: medical management. Coronary angiography already performed during acute PCI usually; additional testing guides management.

metadata.topic: Ischemia Testing and Viability Assessment Post-MI

text: Post-MI depression: 20-30% incidence, associated with poor outcomes, reduced adherence, increased mortality. Screening: PHQ-9 or Depression Anxiety Stress Scale. Intervention: cognitive-behavioral therapy, exercise (proven effective), SSRIs if moderate-severe (sertraline, citalopram; avoid tricyclics). Anxiety common; treated similarly. Participation in cardiac rehab provides psychosocial support. Psychological distress predicts adverse outcomes; addressing mental health integral to secondary prevention.

metadata.topic: Depression Screening and Mental Health Post-MI

text: Post-MI long-term follow-up: cardiology visits at 1-2 weeks, 4-6 weeks, then 3-6 months, then annually. Assess: medication adherence, side effects, symptoms of heart failure/angina, functional status, risk factor control. Medication adherence critical: dual antiplatelet therapy adherence 50% at 12 months without intervention. Interventions: simplify regimen (once-daily dosing), patient education, reminder systems, medication reconciliation. Non-adherence is major cause of stent thrombosis, recurrent events, poor outcomes. Regular follow-up improves adherence and identifies problems early.

COPD: progressive airflow obstruction due to emphysema (alveolar destruction) and chronic bronchitis (airway inflammation). Diagnosis: FEV1/FVC <0.70 on spirometry post-bronchodilator. Risk: smoking (85%), alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, air pollution. GOLD staging (A-D): based on FEV1 % predicted and exacerbation frequency. Pathophysiology: oxidative stress, inflammation, parenchymal destruction, airway collapse on expiration (air trapping). Hypoxemia, hypercapnia (type 2 respiratory failure) in advanced disease.

Asthma: reversible airflow obstruction, bronchial hyperresponsiveness. Phenotypes: allergic (IgE-mediated, atopy history), non-allergic (occupational, irritants), exercise-induced, aspirin-exacerbated (NSAID sensitivity). Severity: intermittent, mild persistent, moderate persistent, severe persistent. Diagnosis: spirometry (FEV1 improvement >12% post-bronchodilator), PEF variability, positive bronchial challenge. Triggers: allergens, cold air, exercise, respiratory infections, stress, GERD.

COPD exacerbation: worsening dyspnea, increased sputum, color change (suggests infection), ±chest discomfort. Triggers: infection (50-75%, bacterial/viral), pollutants, non-adherence, cardiac causes (pulmonary edema mimics). Presenting: tachypnea, tachycardia, accessory muscle use, wheezing/decreased air movement, cyanosis in severe cases. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia (respiratory acidosis), elevated lactate if severe. Chest X-ray: rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, cardiac disease.

metadata.topic: Acute COPD Exacerbation - Triggers and Presentation

text: Asthma exacerbation severity: mild (PEF >70% predicted, accessory muscle use absent/mild, speech normal), moderate (PEF 40-70%, accessory muscle use present, speech interrupted), severe (PEF <40%, severe accessory muscle use, speaks in words/phrases). Danger signs: no wheezing (severe airway obstruction, silent chest), altered mental status (CO2 narcosis), peak flow <25% predicted. SpO2 <90% concerning. Triggers: allergens, infections, exercise, stress, medication non-adherence, cold/dry air. Differential: anaphylaxis, PE, pneumothorax, vocal cord dysfunction.

Beta-2 agonists (albuterol, levalbuterol): rapid bronchodilation via smooth muscle relaxation. Short-acting (SABA, albuterol) onset 5 min, duration 4-6 hours, used as rescue. Long-acting (LABA, salmeterol, formoterol) 12-24 hour duration, maintenance therapy. Anticholinergics (ipratropium, tiotropium): block vagal cholinergic stimulation. LAMA (long-acting muscarinic agonist) maintenance, SAMA (short-acting) rescue. Combination therapy (SABA + SAMA) often used in exacerbations. Side effects: tachycardia, tremor (beta-2), dry mouth (anticholinergic). LABA monotherapy should not be used in asthma (mortality risk).

Corticosteroids (prednisone, methylprednisolone): anti-inflammatory, reduce airway edema. Acute exacerbation: prednisone 40-60 mg daily x 5-7 days (no taper needed if <2 weeks), or methylprednisolone 125 mg IV q6h x 3 days. High-dose short-duration preferred over long course/taper. Benefits: reduced hospitalization, improved FEV1, reduced exacerbation relapse. Side effects: hyperglycemia, mood changes, GI upset. Long-term: increased infection, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression risk. Inhaled ICS (fluticasone, budesonide) maintenance therapy without systemic side effects.

IV magnesium sulfate: smooth muscle relaxant, used in severe asthma exacerbation (PEF <40% predicted, poor response to initial bronchodilators). Dosing: 2g IV over 20 minutes, may repeat. Mechanism: calcium antagonist, enhances beta-2 response. Efficacy debated; some trials show benefit, others don't. Consider in life-threatening asthma (with albuterol, anticholinergics, steroids). Side effects: flushing, hypotension, hypermagnesemia (check Mg level). Contraindications: renal insufficiency, hypocalcemia.

Leukotriene receptor antagonists (montelukast, zafirlukast): block cysteinyl-leukotriene effects (bronchospasm, mucus, inflammation). Used for mild persistent asthma, exercise-induced, allergic rhinitis. Efficacy modest vs ICS/LABA. Neuropsychiatric warning (rare). Omalizumab: anti-IgE monoclonal antibody, blocks mast cell/basophil IgE-mediated activation. Used for moderate-severe allergic asthma (IgE 30-700 IU/mL). SC injection monthly. Expensive, requires monitoring (anaphylaxis risk). Both steroid-sparing agents but no mortality benefit.

metadata.topic: Leukotriene Inhibitors and IgE Monoclonal Antibodies

text: BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure): non-invasive positive pressure ventilation, reduces need for intubation in COPD exacerbation with hypercapnic respiratory failure (pH <7.35, pCO2 >45). Settings: IPAP 8-12 cmH2O (inspiratory), EPAP 3-5 cmH2O (expiratory). Improves CO2 clearance via increased minute ventilation. Success 50-80% if started early (tiring patient = intubation indication). Contraindications: altered mental status (aspiration risk), respiratory muscle fatigue, active GI bleed, facial/airway trauma. Comfort critical; ramp settings, frequent patient reassurance.

Theophylline: methylxanthine bronchodilator, weak beta-2 agonist, phosphodiesterase inhibitor, diuretic. Narrow therapeutic window (10-20 mcg/mL), susceptible to drug interactions (CYP1A2, CYP3A4). Side effects: nausea, vomiting, arrhythmias, seizures (toxicity). Toxicity risk with: hepatic disease, heart failure, concurrent drugs, smoking cessation (levels rise). Limited role; avoided in acute exacerbation (unpredictable absorption/toxicity). Minimal efficacy vs modern bronchodilators. Largely replaced by long-acting bronchodilators. May have role in nocturnal COPD symptoms (long-acting form).

metadata.topic: Theophylline - Limited Modern Use and Toxicity

text: Indications for intubation in COPD/asthma: altered mental status (can't protect airway), severe respiratory distress despite aggressive therapy, apnea/respiratory arrest, fatigue (can't sustain ventilation), worsening blood gas (rising pCO2, falling pH), hypoxemia refractory to supplemental O2, hemodynamic instability. Avoid delaying intubation (causes cardiac arrest); earlier intervention better in severe/unstable patients. Permissive hypercapnia acceptable post-intubation (avoid barotrauma). Sedation/paralysis needed. Weaning: assess readiness daily (decreased sedation, improving gas exchange, tolerating lower ventilator support).

Oxygen therapy: goal SpO2 88-92% in COPD (avoid high SpO2 = CO2 retention via Haldane effect), 94-98% in asthma. Long-term home O2: improves survival if used ≥15 hours/day (NOTT, MRC trials), especially resting hypoxemia (PaO2 <55 mmHg or SaO2 <88%). Supplemental O2 in exacerbations: titrate to SpO2 target, monitor ABG for hypercapnia. Complications: CO2 retention (reduced hypoxic ventilatory drive in COPD), absorption atelectasis, dry airway secretions (humidify). Mask/nasal cannula tolerance important for adherence.

Discharge criteria from exacerbation: improved lung function, able to eat/drink, stable vitals, on target O2, medication instructions understood, reliable follow-up arranged. Pulmonary rehabilitation (exercise training, education, psychosocial support) post-exacerbation improves functional capacity, reduces readmissions 30-40%. Components: aerobic exercise (walking, cycling), resistance training, breathing techniques, education (inhaler technique, smoking cessation, medication adherence), psychological support. Benefits last 6-12 months; ongoing maintenance helpful. Smoking cessation critical; pharmacotherapy (varenicline, bupropion) improves cessation rates.

Vaccinations in COPD: pneumococcal (PCV13 then PPSV23 after 1 year, then PPSV23 every 5 years), influenza annual. Reduces hospitalization/mortality 50%+. Influenza vaccine LAIV contraindicated in COPD (COPD = chronic lung disease). Tdap booster (whooping cough = severe in COPD). RSV vaccine now available (AREXVY, ABRYSVO) for adults ≥60; reduces RSV-associated LRTD. COVID-19 vaccination critical (severe disease risk in COPD). Discuss benefits/risks per patient risk profile.

metadata.topic: Vaccination in COPD - Pneumococcal and Influenza

text: Common mimics of COPD/asthma exacerbation: PE (tachycardia, hypoxemia, unilateral leg swelling, D-dimer elevation), pneumonia (fever, infiltrate, productive cough), pneumothorax (acute onset, hyperresonance, absent breath sounds), acute heart failure (orthopnea, JVP elevation, S3 gallop, crackles), acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, ECG changes, troponin elevation), anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, hypotension, stridor). History, examination, CXR, ECG, troponin help differentiate. COPD/asthma diagnosis not sufficient without excluding dangerous mimics.

metadata.topic: Differential Diagnosis - Not All Dyspnea is COPD/Asthma

text: Type 1 DM: autoimmune beta-cell destruction, absolute insulin deficiency. Incidence peaks age 5-7 and 10-14 years but can occur at any age. Presentation: polydipsia, polyuria, weight loss, fatigue. Ketosis-prone (risk DKA). C-peptide absent/low. Autoantibodies (anti-GAD, anti-islet cell, anti-IA2) present. Risk: family history (HLA-DR3/DR4), other autoimmune diseases (Hashimoto, celiac, Addison). Lifelong insulin dependence required. Complications: hypoglycemia more frequent than Type 2, retinopathy/nephropathy/neuropathy/CAD common.

Type 2 DM: insulin resistance + progressive beta-cell dysfunction. Incidence 90-95% of diabetes. Risk: obesity, age >45, family history, physical inactivity, ethnicity (Hispanic, African American, Asian American, Native American). Metabolic syndrome (obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia) common. Presents insidiously; often asymptomatic at diagnosis (found on screening). C-peptide normal/high initially (preserved secretion). Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥126, HbA1c ≥6.5%, OGTT ≥200. Non-insulin dependence initially but may require insulin long-term (beta-cell failure).

metadata.topic: Type 2 Diabetes - Pathophysiology and Risk Factors

text: Gestational DM: glucose intolerance first recognized in pregnancy (not pre-existing). Incidence 2-10% pregnancies. Risk: age, obesity, family history, prior GDM, PCOS. Screening: 50g OGCT at 24-28 weeks; if ≥140, proceed to 3-hour OGTT. Diagnosis: ≥2 abnormal values on OGTT. Management: dietary counseling (carb counting), exercise, insulin often needed (metformin/glyburide safer than other agents in pregnancy). Increases risk gestational HTN, preeclampsia, macrosomia, neonatal hypoglycemia. 50% develop Type 2 DM within 5 years postpartum.

Diagnostic criteria: fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL (no calories x8h), random glucose ≥200 with symptoms, HbA1c ≥6.5% (glycosylated hemoglobin, 2-3 month glucose average), 2-hour glucose ≥200 on OGTT (75g glucose load). Prediabetes: fasting 100-125, HbA1c 5.7-6.4%. HbA1c advantages: no fasting required, reflects long-term control. Limitations: hemolytic anemia (false low), hemoglobin variants affect accuracy. Values repeat for confirmation (except symptomatic hyperglycemia). Self-monitoring: home glucose logs, continuous glucose monitors (CGM).

metadata.topic: Diabetes Diagnosis - HbA1c, Fasting Glucose, OGTT

text: HbA1c targets individualized: <7% for non-fragile adults (lower risk, good functional status). <8% for fragile elderly, limited life expectancy, hypoglycemia-prone. <6.5% controversial in Type 2 (increased mortality in some trials, intensive therapy-related). Very high targets (8-9%) acceptable if severe hypoglycemia, limited access, advanced complications. Factors: age, comorbidities, hypoglycemia awareness, medication burden, renal/liver disease. Adjust targets at 3-6 month intervals based on HbA1c, patient tolerance, hypoglycemia frequency. Patient preference critical; shared decision-making preferred over rigid targets.

Metformin (biguanide): first-line agent for Type 2 DM. Mechanism: decreases hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis), improves insulin sensitivity. Benefits: weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, cardiovascular benefit, rhabdomyolysis rare. Dosing: 500-2000 mg daily (BID-TID, extended-release available). Contraindication: GFR <30 (risk lactic acidosis from accumulation); caution if GFR 30-45. Side effects: GI (nausea, diarrhea, 30% patients), vitamin B12 deficiency (monitor annually), lactic acidosis (very rare if renal function normal). Iodinated contrast: hold metformin 48h after contrast (risk acute renal injury + lactic acidosis), restart if renal function stable.

Sulfonylureas (glyburide, glipizide, glimepiride): increase insulin secretion. Mechanism: block ATP-sensitive K+ channels on beta cells, increase insulin release. Benefits: effective glucose lowering (HbA1c -1-2%), inexpensive, oral. Risk: hypoglycemia (15-20% vs 5% with metformin), weight gain, secondary failure (beta-cell exhaustion). Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): similar mechanism, shorter-acting, pre-meal dosing. Lower hypoglycemia risk than sulfonylureas but still present. Both contraindicated if recurrent hypoglycemia, hypoglycemia unawareness, renal/hepatic disease. Preference shifted to newer agents (SGLT2i, GLP-1) with cardiovascular/renal benefits.

SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin): block renal glucose reabsorption, increase urinary glucose excretion. Benefits: HbA1c -0.5-1%, weight loss, blood pressure reduction, cardiovascular mortality reduction (EMPA-REG OUTCOME, CANVAS), heart failure benefit, CKD slowing. Side effects: genital mycotic infection (10%), diabetic ketoacidosis (euglycemic DKA if SGLT2i), dehydration (diuretic effect), amputation risk (canagliflozin, less with other agents). Contraindication: DKA (or euglycemic DKA risk), type 1 DM (euglycemic DKA risk), severe renal disease (GFR <20). Monitor volume status, renal function. Advantageous in CKD, heart failure, obesity.

metadata.topic: SGLT2 Inhibitors - Cardiovascular and Renal Benefits

text: GLP-1 agonists (liraglutide, dulaglutide, semaglutide, tirzepatide): incretin mimetics, increase insulin secretion (glucose-dependent), slow gastric emptying, reduce appetite. Benefits: HbA1c -1-1.8%, weight loss 2-5 kg, cardiovascular mortality reduction, GFR stabilization. Side effects: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea (40%), pancreatitis risk (controversial), thyroid C-cell tumors (animal studies; unknown human risk). Contraindication: personal/family history medullary thyroid cancer, MEN-2 syndrome, acute pancreatitis. Injection weekly (some agents). Cost barrier in some regions. Superior to other agents in weight loss, CV benefit.

metadata.topic: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists - Weight Loss and CV Protection

text: DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin): enhance endogenous GLP-1 by blocking dipeptidyl peptidase-4. Benefits: modest glucose lowering (HbA1c -0.5-0.8%), weight-neutral, no hypoglycemia, oral daily dosing, well-tolerated. Drawbacks: less effective than metformin or GLP-1, no CV/renal benefit clear. Useful in renal disease (linagliptin preferred). Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone, rosiglitazone): insulin sensitizers, increase adipose glucose uptake. Benefits: HbA1c -1-1.5%, CV benefit (pioglitazone in high-risk Type 2). Drawbacks: weight gain, fluid retention (HF risk), bone loss, bladder cancer risk (pioglitazone, controlled). Rarely first-line now; reserved for specific indications.

Insulin types: rapid-acting (aspart, lispro, glulisine, 5-15 min onset), short-acting (regular, 30-60 min), intermediate (NPH, 2-4 hours), long-acting (glargine U100, degludec U200, 24 hours). Regimens: basal-bolus (long-acting basal daily + rapid-acting with meals) preferred for Type 1; sliding scale (rapid-acting per glucose readings) less preferred (reactive not proactive). Dosing: 0.5-1 unit/kg daily split basal/bolus (50% each); adjust by 2-4 units every 3 days per glucose logs/HbA1c. Premix insulin (70/30 NPH/regular, 75/25 lispro/protamine): convenient x2 daily but less flexible. Insulin pump (continuous SC infusion) for Type 1, selected Type 2.

metadata.topic: Insulin Types and Regimens - Basal-Bolus Strategy

text: Hypoglycemia: glucose <70 mg/dL. Symptoms: tremor, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, hunger (adrenergic), confusion, slurred speech, seizure (neuroglycopenic). Symptomatic <70 treated immediately. Rule of 15: 15g carbohydrate (4 oz juice, 3-4 dextrose tablets, 1 tbsp honey), recheck at 15 minutes, repeat if still <100. Follow with long-acting carbohydrate (bread, milk). Severe hypoglycemia (seizure, LOC): glucagon 1mg IM/IV, then carbohydrates when able. Prevention: patient education, frequent monitoring (CGM), realistic targets, medication adjustment. Hypoglycemia unawareness (loss of adrenergic warning): risk with long-standing diabetes, tight control, autonomic neuropathy; requires relaxed targets.

DKA (diabetic ketoacidosis): acute life-threatening condition with: pH <7.3, HCO3- <15, elevated ketones (beta-hydroxybutyrate >3), anion gap metabolic acidosis. Pathophysiology: insulin deficiency leads to hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, dehydration; free fatty acid mobilization leads to ketone production. Usually Type 1 but can occur Type 2. Triggers: infection (50%), non-adherence, new-onset diabetes, medications (steroids, SGLT2i). Presentation: polydipsia, polyuria, Kussmaul respirations (deep rapid breathing, fruity breath from acetone), nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, altered mental status (more severe hyperglycemia/hyperosmolality). Mortality 1-5% if treated, >15% if delayed.

DKA treatment: (1) IV fluids: 0.9% NS 500-1000 mL/hr initially (aggressive hydration), switch to 0.45% NS once glucose <250. Total deficit typically 5-10L. (2) Insulin: bolus 0.1 units/kg IV, then 0.1 units/kg/hr continuous infusion (usually 5-10 units/hr), titrate to reduce glucose 50-75 mg/dL/hr. (3) Potassium: check baseline; likely total body deficit 3-5 mEq/kg despite normal/high serum K+ (shifts). Replete cautiously (K+ shift into cells with insulin = hypokalemia risk). (4) Bicarbonate: controversial, reserved for pH <6.9 (3 amps NaHCO3 in D5W). Monitor: glucose, electrolytes, ABG q1-2h initially, neuro checks. Switch to SC insulin once ketosis resolves (glucose <200, HCO3- >15, eating).

metadata.topic: DKA Treatment - Fluids, Insulin, Electrolyte Repletion

text: HHS (hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state): acute hyperglycemic emergency, usually Type 2 (older, renal/cardiac comorbidities). Diagnostic: glucose >600 mg/dL, osmolality >320 (calculated = 2[Na] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8), minimal/absent ketonemia (pH usually >7.30, HCO3- >15), often altered mental status. Triggers: infection, medication non-adherence, medications (steroids, antipsychotics). More common in older patients, higher mortality (15-20% even treated) than DKA. Pathophysiology: residual insulin prevents ketosis but cannot lower glucose; severe hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis, severe dehydration. Treatment similar to DKA but slower glucose reduction (25-50 mg/dL/hr risk osmotic edema/stroke), more aggressive fluid repletion, insulin lower-dose.

Sick day management: increase glucose monitoring (q2-4h), stay hydrated, take medications as usual (especially insulin; never stop). Hyperglycemia response: if glucose >250, check for DKA/HHS signs. Hypoglycemia: treat per protocol. Nausea/vomiting: small frequent meals/liquids, antiemetics, IV fluids if severe. Hospital glycemic control: target 140-180 mg/dL (lower targets increase hypoglycemia risk). Insulin-only regimens (hold other agents): basal-bolus IV insulin (0.5 units/kg/24h basal, additional bolus per carb intake). Subcutaneous insulin resumption when: eating, hemodynamically stable, not in DKA/HHS. Avoid hypoglycemia <70 (impairs recovery, increases infection risk, cardiovascular events).

metadata.topic: Sick Day Management and Glycemic Control in Hospital

text: Retinopathy: nonproliferative (microaneurysms, dot-blot hemorrhages) to proliferative (neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment). Screening: annual dilated eye exam. Treatment: tight glucose/BP control, laser photocoagulation, anti-VEGF injections. Nephropathy: early albuminuria, progressing to chronic kidney disease, end-stage renal disease. Screening: urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, eGFR. Prevention: tight glucose control, ACE-I/ARB (renal protection), SGLT2i. Neuropathy: distal sensory polyneuropathy (loss protective sensation, ulcer risk), autonomic (orthostatic HTN, erectile dysfunction, gastroparesis). Management: glucose control, gabapentin, pregabalin for pain. Screening: annual monofilament testing, vibration sense, ankle reflexes.

CAD: diabetes increases risk 2-4 fold, multiple infarcts possible, silent ischemia common. Screening: EKG baseline, stress testing if high risk, CAC score controversial. Treatment: aggressive lipid/BP control, dual antiplatelet therapy post-event, revascularization if indicated. Stroke: atherosclerotic and cardioembolic mechanisms. Increased risk with diabetes + HTN + dyslipidemia. Prevention: aspirin, tight BP/lipid/glucose control, carotid imaging if symptomatic. Peripheral artery disease (PAD): claudication, critical limb ischemia, amputation risk. Treatment: walking program, cilostazol, revascularization, foot care (prevent ulcers). Aggressive risk factor modification decreases CV events 20-50%.

UGIB: bleeding proximal to ligament of Treitz (esophagus, stomach, duodenum, proximal jejunum). Incidence 50-100 per 100,000 annually. Mortality 5-15% (higher in elderly, comorbidities). Presenting as hematemesis (bright red or coffee ground), melena (black tarry stools, suggests proximal source), or positive nasogastric tube aspirate. Severity: vital sign abnormalities (tachycardia, hypotension), altered mental status indicate significant blood loss.

metadata.topic: Upper GI Bleed (UGIB) Epidemiology and Presentation

text: PUD: gastric or duodenal ulcers (20-30% of UGIB). Risk factors: H. pylori infection (90% risk if colonized), NSAIDs (20-30% long-term users), stress ulcers (surgery, sepsis, mechanical ventilation), PPI use (rare). Pathophysiology: mucosal erosion >2mm, through submucosa into mucosa. Presents with epigastric pain (may be absent in elderly), GI bleed, perforation (pain, free air, peritonitis). Diagnosis: EGD with ulcer visualization. Duodenal ulcers more common than gastric, less likely to malignancy.

metadata.topic: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) - Risk Factors and Pathophysiology

text: Variceal bleeding: occurs if portal pressure gradient >12 mmHg (hepatic encephalopathy/portal vein gradient measurement). Incidence in cirrhosis: 5-15% yearly if varices present. Mortality: 20-50% first bleed if untreated, 15% with treatment. Presentation: massive hematemesis, hypotension, shock (often rapid exsanguination). Risk factors: Child-Pugh score, bilirubin, INR, variceal size, red signs on endoscopy. Prognosis: depends on liver synthetic function, etiology (variceal bleeding worse than non-variceal in cirrhosis).

metadata.topic: Variceal Bleeding in Cirrhosis - Pathophysiology and Outcomes

text: Esophagitis: inflammation from reflux (GERD), caustic ingestion, infection (CMV/HSV in immunocompromised). Presents with dysphagia, chest pain. Mallory-Weiss tear: mucosal laceration at GE junction from forceful vomiting (especially alcohol). Usually self-limited bleeding, 10-15% need intervention. Boerhaave syndrome: full-thickness esophageal rupture (forceful vomiting/straining). Presents with sudden chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, mediastinitis, sepsis. Mortality 10-30% even with surgery; diagnosis with contrast esophagography. Requires emergency surgery.

Gastric cancer: can present as UGIB. Risk: H. pylori, smoking, family history. Diagnosis: EGD with biopsy of gastric ulcer/mass. Portal hypertensive gastropathy: gastric mucosal ectasia in portal hypertension, can bleed. Antral predominance typical. Diagnosis: endoscopy appearance. Treatment differs from varices (less variceal banding effective). Beta-blockers for primary/secondary prophylaxis. Gastric cancer managed with surgery/oncology consultation.

metadata.topic: Gastric Cancer and Portal Hypertensive Gastropathy

text: Initial UGIB management: place 2 large-bore IVs, type and cross, CBC/CMP/coagulation, lactate. Supplemental O2 if hypoxic. NPO status. Continuous cardiac monitoring. Contact GI for urgent endoscopy (within 24 hours standard, <1 hour if variceal/massive). Nasogastric tube (check for blood, helps confirm UGIB location). Pharmacotherapy: PPI bolus 80mg IV, then infusion 8 mg/hr for PUD. Octreotide 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr infusion for suspected variceal (start before endoscopy if likely).
