Correct coagulopathy if INR >1.5, platelet <50k.

metadata.topic: UGIB Initial Management - Resuscitation and Stabilization

text: Glasgow-Blatchford: predicts need for intervention in UGIB (0-23 points, higher = higher risk). Components: age, sex, shock (pulse, SBP), comorbidity, bleeding (Hgb, melena). Score 0: <5% need intervention; can discharge without endoscopy (selected patients). AIMS65: mortality prediction (age ≥65, INR >1.5, mental status altered, SBP <100, endoscopic findings). Score 0: low mortality (<1%); score >2: high mortality (>20%). Both useful for risk stratification but don't replace clinical judgment. Endoscopy still gold standard for diagnosis/treatment.

metadata.topic: Glasgow-Blatchford Score vs AIMS65 for UGIB Risk Stratification

text: PPI for PUD bleeding: omeprazole 80mg IV bolus, then 8 mg/hr continuous infusion x 72 hours, then PO dose (optimal regimen). High-dose IV PPI reduces rebleeding (5-10% vs 15-20% if not treated), mortality. Duration: continue IV 72h post-endoscopy if PUD visualized, then switch to PO daily x 4 weeks minimum. Confirm H. pylori status; treat if positive (7-14 day triple/quadruple therapy). Stop NSAIDs if possible. Recheck H. pylori eradication 4 weeks post-treatment (confirm success). PPIs generally safe; long-term use risks: hypomagnesemia, C. difficile, vitamin B12 deficiency.

metadata.topic: Proton Pump Inhibitor (PPI) Therapy in UGIB

text: Octreotide (somatostatin analog): reduces portal pressure, controls variceal bleeding in 80% cases. Dosing: 50 mcg IV bolus, then 50 mcg/hr continuous infusion x 2-5 days. Start BEFORE endoscopy if variceal bleeding suspected. Antibiotics in variceal bleeding: ceftriaxone 1g IV daily (preferred) or norfloxacin 400mg PO BID x 7 days. Reduces bacterial infection (SBP, bacteremia), mortality 20-30%. Mechanism: gut sterilization, reduced translocation. Must start with octreotide/endoscopic therapy, not antibiotics alone.

metadata.topic: Octreotide and Antibiotics in Variceal Bleeding

text: Endoscopic hemostasis (gold standard for UGIB management): (1) Injection: epinephrine 1:10,000 (4-10 mL submucosal injection around bleeding vessel), followed by sclerosant (sodium tetradecyl sulfate) or cyanoacrylate. (2) Thermal: electrocautery (bipolar or heater probe), argon plasma coagulation (APC). (3) Mechanical: variceal banding (elastic bands around varices), clips. Success rate 90-95% for PUD, 80-90% for varices. Rebleeding: 10-30% if PUD, 30-50% if varices (may need repeat endoscopy). Two-third of ulcers have visible vessel or clot; these need treatment (active bleeding vs oozing). Clean-base ulcers: low rebleeding risk, no intervention.

metadata.topic: Endoscopic Hemostasis Techniques - Injection, Thermal, Banding

text: Rebleeding risk factors: large ulcer (>2cm), location (posterior duodenal = high risk, gastric body/fundus = high risk), visible vessel/active bleeding, hemodynamic instability. Surgical consultation if: failure of endoscopic hemostasis (second attempt if first fails, 80% success; >2 failed attempts = surgical consideration), massive transfusion requirement (>6 units/8 hours), hemodynamic instability despite resuscitation, perforation suspected. Surgical options: antrectomy ± vagotomy (PUD), oversewing vessel ± transfusion, partial gastrectomy (gastric cancer). Mortality surgery 10-30%.

metadata.topic: Rebleeding Risk Stratification and Surgical Consult Indications

text: Restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse PRBCs target Hgb 7-9 g/dL (not 10 g/dL as historically). Benefits: reduce transfusion volume, fewer complications (infection, ARDS, volume overload), lower mortality in some trials. Apply in stable patients; transfuse more liberally if: active bleeding, cardiac disease, ongoing hemorrhage, Hgb <7. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP): only if INR >1.5 (NOT for Hgb <10 alone). Platelets if <50k and actively bleeding. Avoid coagulopathy over-correction (increases thrombotic risk). Consider massive transfusion protocol if >4 units RBC/hour (include FFP, platelets in 1:1:1 ratio).

metadata.topic: Transfusion Strategy in UGIB - Restrictive vs Liberal

text: TIPS: radiologic procedure creating shunt between portal vein and hepatic vein to reduce portal pressure. Indications in variceal bleeding: refractory bleeding (failure of variceal banding + octreotide + antibiotics, <20% of cases), as bridge to transplant, prophylaxis for recurrent bleeding despite banding. Timing: within 24-48 hours of failed endoscopy. Contraindications: encephalopathy (worsens with TIPS), right heart failure, portal vein thrombosis. Complications: shunt thrombosis (40% by 1 year, treated with thrombolysis/revision), encephalopathy (30%), hepatic decompensation. Reduces mortality vs repeat bleeds but transplantation ultimately definitive for decompensated cirrhosis.

LGIB: bleeding distal to ligament of Treitz (colon, rectum). Incidence 20-30 per 100,000 annually. Mortality 2-4%. Etiologies: diverticulosis (30-40%), internal hemorrhoids (15-25%), angiodysplasia (5-10%), IBD (Crohn's, UC, 5-10%), ischemic colitis (5%), infectious colitis (C. difficile, etc, 3-5%). Presentation: bright red blood per rectum (hematochezia) or maroon stools. 90% LGIB self-limited; 15% require intervention (emergency endoscopy/colonoscopy/angiography).

metadata.topic: Lower GI Bleed (LGIB) Epidemiology and Etiologies

text: Diverticulosis: outpouchings of colon mucosa (especially sigmoid, low-fiber diet risk). Most asymptomatic; 10-20% develop diverticulitis (inflammation/microperforation). Presentation in diverticulitis: LLQ pain, fever, diarrhea, leukocytosis. Diverticular bleeding: painless, brisk (bright red or maroon), usually self-limited. Diagnosis: colonoscopy (shows diverticula, rules out other causes), CT if perforation suspected (free air, pericolonic stranding). Management: no specific treatment for uncomplicated diverticulosis (no prophylactic antibiotics recommended); diverticulitis = antibiotics ± percutaneous drainage if abscess; avoid colonoscopy during active inflammation (perforation risk).

metadata.topic: Diverticulosis and Diverticulitis - Distinction and Management

text: Crohn's disease: transmural inflammation (any part GI tract, 40% small bowel), cobblestone appearance, skip lesions, fistulas/strictures. Ulcerative colitis: mucosal/submucosal inflammation (colon/rectum only), continuous involvement, pseudopolyps. Both can present with GI bleed (usually chronic rather than massive). Extraintestinal manifestations: joint pain, uveitis, erythema nodosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis. Diagnosis: endoscopy + biopsy (granulomas in Crohn's, crypt distortion UC). Management: corticosteroids, aminosalicylates (mesalamine), immune modulators (azathioprine, 6-MP), anti-TNF biologics (infliximab, adalimumab), surgical resection if refractory.

metadata.topic: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD) - Crohn's vs Ulcerative Colitis

text: Angiodysplasia: small submucosal vascular malformations, right colon predominance. Risk: advanced age, aortic stenosis, renal failure (uremic toxins damage vessels). Presents with chronic GI bleeding (may cause iron-deficiency anemia, obscure GI bleed if small). Diagnosis: colonoscopy (appears as spider-web vessels, cherry-red lesions) or capsule endoscopy. Endoscopic hemostasis: argon plasma coagulation (APC), electrocautery, injection, clips. Angiographic embolization if endoscopy fails. Prone to recurrence; may require repeat interventions. Chronic anticoagulation increases bleeding risk.

Ischemic colitis: reduced colonic blood flow (usually right or left colon, sparing rectum which has dual blood supply). Risk: age >60, cardiovascular disease, hypotension, arrhythmias, hypercoagulable state. Presentation: acute abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, fever. Mild-moderate: mucosal ulceration; severe: transmural necrosis (perforation risk). Diagnosis: colonoscopy (pale, cyanotic mucosa, ulcers), CT (thumbprinting sign, wall thickening). Management: supportive (IV fluids, antibiotics if septic), NPO, surgery if perforation/peritonitis. Prognosis: 80% improve with supportive care; 20% progress to fulminant disease/death.

metadata.topic: Ischemic Colitis - Pathophysiology and Clinical Presentation

text: C. difficile: leading cause antibiotic-associated colitis; toxins A/B damage mucosa, 5-10% develop toxic megacolon/perforation. Risk: antibiotics, age >65, immunosuppression, hospitalization. Presentation: watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, elevated creatinine. Diagnosis: stool PCR for toxin genes (most sensitive), or toxin enzyme immunoassay. Management: stop offending antibiotic if possible, metronidazole 500mg TID x 10 days (mild-moderate), vancomycin 125mg QID x 10 days (severe: Cr >1.5x baseline, WBC >15k, severe colitis). Fidaxocin if recurrent (lower relapse). Avoid antiperistaltic agents (increase toxic megacolon risk).

metadata.topic: Infectious Colitis - C. difficile and Other Pathogens

text: Internal hemorrhoids: above dentate line, painless (visceral innervation), bright red blood on paper/toilet, may prolapse. External hemorrhoids: below dentate line, painful (somatic innervation), visible/palpable. Diagnosis: visual inspection, anoscopy (internal), digital rectal exam (external). Management: conservative = high-fiber diet, stool softeners, sitz baths. Procedures: rubber-band ligation (internal), sclerotherapy, coagulation. Surgery (hemorrhoidectomy) reserved for refractory cases. Complications: thrombosis (painful, treat with surgical drainage if severe/painful), bleeding (usually self-limited). Not life-threatening but most common cause LGIB.

metadata.topic: Internal and External Hemorrhoids - Distinction and Management

text: Meckel's diverticulum: remnant of vitelline duct (embryologic structure), present in 2% population. Rule of 2's: 2% prevalence, 2 feet from ileocecal valve, 2 inches long, 2% symptomatic. Symptoms: painless GI bleed (bright red, brisk), intestinal obstruction, intussusception, diverticulitis (mimics appendicitis). Contains ectopic tissue: 50% gastric mucosa (produces acid causing ileal ulceration/bleeding). Diagnosis: Meckel scan (technetium-99m pertechnetate binds to gastric mucosa), CT enterography, capsule endoscopy (variable sensitivity). Treatment: surgical resection if symptomatic or symptomatic potential. Bleeding risk highest in children/young adults.

metadata.topic: Meckel's Diverticulum - Classic Presentation and Diagnosis

text: Colonoscopy: gold standard for LGIB diagnosis (90% localize source). Indications: active/recent hematochezia, iron-deficiency anemia, positive FOBT. Timing: urgent (<24 hours) if hemodynamically unstable/high-risk bleeding (variceal equivalent in lower GI = diverticulosis/angiodysplasia in elderly); elective (within 1 week) if stable, minor bleeding. Preparation: bowel prep (GoLYTELY, MiraLAX) critical for visualization. Hemostasis: APC, electrocautery, injection, clips as for UGIB. Success rate: 80-90% of bleeding sources identified and treated. Risks: perforation (0.1%), bleeding complication (0.1%), aspiration.

metadata.topic: Colonoscopy in LGIB - Indications and Timing

text: Obscure GI bleeding: bleeding without identified source on EGD/colonoscopy. Incidence 5-10% LGIB. Capsule endoscopy: wireless camera pill ingested, transmits images. Sensitivity 50-75% for small bowel bleeding (better than push enteroscopy). Limitations: cannot obtain biopsy/perform hemostasis, retained capsule risk if stricture. Video capsule endoscopy can identify angiodysplasia, Meckel's diverticulum, small bowel Crohn's. Enterography: CT or MR enterography shows anatomy, can miss small lesions <2cm. Angiography: if active bleeding (>2 mL/min), can localize and treat (embolization). Capsule endoscopy first-line for obscure LGIB after normal colonoscopy.

metadata.topic: Capsule Endoscopy and Enterography for Obscure GI Bleeding

text: GI bleeding in anticoagulated patients: increase mortality/complications. Management: resuscitate, obtain hemostasis endoscopically. Reverse anticoagulation if major bleed: warfarin = FFP/PCC + vitamin K (see UGIB section), DOACs = idarucizumab (dabigatran) or andexanet (apixaban/rivaroxaban) if available, LMWH = protamine if recent dose. Risk-benefit: reversing anticoagulation = thrombotic event risk (stroke, MI, PE if original indication was afib/VTE). Hold anticoagulation temporarily (3-5 days) if minor bleed; restart once hemostasis achieved. Discuss with anticoagulation/cardiology team for long-term plan (may resume on different agent/higher dose PPI).

Post-polypectomy hemorrhage: can occur immediately (<24 hours, usually during procedure) or delayed (>24 hours post-polypectomy). Incidence: 1-3% (higher with large polyps, anticoagulation, certain polyp types). Delayed bleeding: patient presents with hematochezia 3-7 days post-procedure. Risk factors: anticoagulation, large polyp (>2cm), antiplatelet therapy. Prevention: pre-procedure clips (prophylactic hemoclips), submucosal epinephrine injection, hot-snare for large polyps. Management: urgent colonoscopy for delayed bleed, repeat endoscopic hemostasis (clips, injection, thermal), transfusion support if needed. Surgery rare (<5%). Resumption of anticoagulation: delayed 5-7 days if minor bleeding, longer if major.

Pulmonary embolism: blood clot obstructing pulmonary arteries. Incidence 60-100 per 100,000 annually. Mortality 2-10% treated, 30% untreated. Virchow's triad: venous stasis (immobility, obesity, surgery), endothelial injury (trauma, central lines, atrial fibrillation), hypercoagulability (malignancy, thrombophilia, estrogen). Risk stratification: massive (hemodynamic instability, RV strain), submassive (RV strain but stable), stable (no RV strain).

Wells score (0-12.5 points): predicts pretest probability PE. Points: PE most likely diagnosis (3), heart rate >100 (1.5), signs of DVT (3), hemoptysis (1), signs of shock (3.5 if hypotensive, 1.5 if syncope), atelectasis/consolidation not lateral (1.5), CXR normal (1.5). Score <2: low risk (1.3% PE). 2-6: moderate risk (16.2% PE). >6: high risk (37.5% PE). If low clinical probability + normal D-dimer: PE ruled out. Used in two-level PE-protocol (Wells + D-dimer).

metadata.topic: Wells Score for PE Clinical Probability

text: D-dimer: marker of thrombin generation/fibrin degradation (high sensitivity, low specificity). Normal D-dimer (<500 ng/mL) has 95-99% negative predictive value for VTE in low-to-moderate pretest probability. Elevated in: PE, DVT, MI, sepsis, DIC, trauma, cancer, pregnancy, postoperative state. Not useful to rule in PE (elevated in many conditions). Age-adjusted cutoff (age × 10 ng/mL) improves specificity in elderly. High D-dimer doesn't require imaging if low clinical suspicion.

CTPA: gold standard for PE diagnosis. Findings: main pulmonary artery (massive PE), lobar (large emboli), segmental (moderate), subsegmental (small, controversial significance). Sensitivity 94-98%, specificity 95-98%. Can detect alternative diagnoses (pneumonia, pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, aortic dissection). Subsegmental PE (SSPE): clinical significance debated; isolated SSPE in hemodynamically stable patient may not require anticoagulation (NEJM 2024). Right heart strain on CT (RV/LV ratio >0.9) prognostically important.

PE presentation: dyspnea (73%), chest pain (52%, often pleuritic), syncope (5%, often massive PE), sudden cardiac arrest (2%, fulminant). Tachycardia, tachypnea common. S1Q3T3 on ECG (classic but rare, 10-15%), more commonly sinus tachycardia/NSR with nonspecific changes. Calf swelling/pain suggests DVT source. Absence of dyspnea doesn't rule out PE; maintain high suspicion. Signs of RV strain/shock indicate massive PE.

metadata.topic: PE - Clinical Presentation and Red Flags

text: ECG: S1Q3T3 (>10% cases), sinus tachycardia, right axis deviation, RV strain pattern (T wave inversion V1-V3, sometimes others). New AFib possible. ECG normal doesn't exclude PE. Troponin elevation: present in 30-50% PE, indicates RV injury, worse prognosis. BNP elevation: indicates RV strain, prognostically important. Neither troponin nor BNP diagnostic for PE; used for risk stratification in confirmed PE (prognostic).

Echocardiography findings in PE: RV dilatation (RV/LV ratio >0.9), RV dysfunction (reduced RV systolic strain), elevated pulmonary artery pressure (TR velocity >2.8 m/s = PA systolic >35), McConnell's sign (RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing, specific for PE). Echo useful to identify RV dysfunction (prognostic), assess for alternative diagnoses (tamponade, perioperative MI), right heart catheterization not routinely needed. Normal echo doesn't exclude PE (may be normal in subsegmental PE).

metadata.topic: Echocardiography in PE - RV Strain Assessment

text: Massive PE: systemic hypotension (SBP <90 for >15 min) or shock (lactate >2, oliguria, altered mental status), high mortality 30-50%. Requires thrombolysis or embolectomy. Submassive PE: hemodynamically stable but with RV dysfunction (echo findings, elevated troponin/BNP), mortality 5-10%, intermediate therapy considered. Stable PE: no RV dysfunction, normal troponin/BNP, mortality <5%, anticoagulation alone sufficient. Risk stratification guides therapy (anticoagulation vs thrombolysis vs mechanical intervention).

metadata.topic: Massive PE vs Submassive PE vs Stable PE

text: Ventilation-perfusion scans: historically used for PE diagnosis, largely replaced by CTPA. Still used if: contrast allergy, renal insufficiency, pregnancy (lower radiation/iodine exposure). Findings: normal (PE excluded), low probability, intermediate probability (inconclusive), high probability. Low + low clinical suspicion = PE excluded. High + high clinical suspicion = PE confirmed. Intermediate results + discordant clinical probability = need CTPA or D-dimer.

Screening for asymptomatic PE (incidental pulmonary emboli) controversial. Found on 1-2% of CT angiographies for other indications. Most isolated subsegmental PEs in asymptomatic patients don't require anticoagulation (low bleeding risk outweighs benefit). Treatment depends: main/lobar PE = anticoagulate even if asymptomatic; segmental = consider clinical context (cancer, hypercoagulable state); subsegmental = usually observe. High clinical judgment needed; avoid reflexively treating incidental PE.

metadata.topic: PE Screening in Asymptomatic Patients - When to Consider

text: PE in pregnancy: increased risk (especially third trimester/postpartum), mortality higher. Dyspnea/tachycardia harder to distinguish from normal pregnancy. Imaging: CTPA relatively safe (fetal radiation <1 rad); V/Q scan alternative if contrast allergy (higher fetal risk than CTPA). Anticoagulation: LMWH preferred (doesn't cross placenta), UFH also safe. Warfarin avoided (teratogenic first trimester, fetal hemorrhage risk). Thrombolysis reserved for massive PE (maternal mortality >25%). IVC filter if anticoagulation contraindicated.

Deep vein thrombosis: clot in leg veins (popliteal, femoral, iliac). Incidence 1-2 per 1000 annually. Risk: immobilization (surgery, paralysis), malignancy, thrombophilia, recent surgery/trauma, central lines, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, hormone therapy. Virchow's triad applies. Complications: pulmonary embolism (10-50% untreated), post-thrombotic syndrome (20-50%), recurrent thrombosis if untreated.

Wells score DVT (0-8 points): clinical suspicion before ultrasound. Points: active cancer (1), leg immobilization (1), recent surgery requiring general anesthesia (1), calf swelling >3cm vs other (1), pitting edema unilateral (1), collateral superficial veins (1), entire leg swelling (1), localized tenderness along deep veins (1), alternative diagnosis likely (-2). Score 0-1: low risk (5% DVT). 2-6: moderate risk (17% DVT). >6: high risk (53% DVT). Very low score + normal D-dimer = DVT excluded.

metadata.topic: Wells Score for DVT Clinical Probability

text: Compression ultrasound: gold standard for DVT diagnosis. Sensitivity/specificity >95%. Technique: apply probe pressure (compress veins); thrombus = vein doesn't collapse completely. Exam limited if: severe edema, bandages, pain, obesity (operator-dependent). Proximal DVT (popliteal, femoral, iliac): single abnormal US diagnostic. Distal DVT (calf veins): if negative, repeat in 5-7 days if high suspicion (20% propagate proximally). MRI/CT if ultrasound inconclusive or IVC suspected involved.

metadata.topic: Compression Ultrasound - DVT Diagnosis Gold Standard

text: DVT presentation: unilateral leg edema/swelling (most common), calf pain/tenderness, erythema, warmth. Homan's sign (calf pain with dorsiflexion) and Pratt's sign (adductor tenderness) not specific. Phlegmasia: severe DVT with compromised venous return, cyanosis, severe pain, skin necrosis (emergency). Bilateral swelling: suggests IVC involvement or medical causes (heart failure, renal disease). Absence of symptoms doesn't exclude DVT (20% asymptomatic in hospitalized patients).

Superficial venous thrombosis (SVT): clot in superficial veins (saphenous, tributaries). Presents with cord-like tenderness, erythema, pain along vein path. Lower risk of PE (1-3%) vs DVT. Management: anticoagulation if: >5cm from saphenofemoral junction, involves saphenofemoral junction, concurrent DVT, malignancy, thrombophilia. Otherwise: NSAIDs, compression, early mobilization may suffice. Duplex ultrasound confirms diagnosis and assesses proximity to deep system. Repeat US in 1 week if SVT extends toward saphenofemoral junction.

Inferior vena cava (IVC) thrombosis: rare but serious, risk of massive PE, bilaterally compromised perfusion. Causes: IVC filter, malignancy invading IVC, primary thrombosis (thrombophilia), hypercoagulable state. Presentation: bilateral leg edema, dilated superficial veins (collateral), pain. Diagnosis: CT with contrast or duplex ultrasound of IVC. Management: anticoagulation (UFH preferred if IVC filter removal needed), consider thrombolysis if massive. Prognosis: depends on extent, cause; recurrence risk high without addressing underlying cause.

Provoked DVT (surgery, immobilization, cancer, trauma): anticoagulation 3 months if reversible risk, longer (6-12 months) if malignancy. Unprovoked DVT (no clear precipitant): anticoagulation ≥3 months; extended therapy (indefinite) if recurrent VTE, cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, thrombophilia, or inadequate anticoagulation. D-dimer after stopping anticoagulation: if positive, increased recurrence risk (guides extended therapy decision). Male sex, proximal DVT, RV dysfunction, elevated D-dimer suggest higher recurrence risk.

metadata.topic: VTE Risk Stratification for Anticoagulation Duration

text: LMWH (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h): outpatient treatment, predictable pharmacokinetics, no monitoring required, good for most patients. UFH IV (80 units/kg bolus, then infusion 18 units/kg/hr): inpatient, used if renal failure (CrCl <30), need for rapid reversal, or embolectomy planned. DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): oral, avoid if severe renal disease, pregnancy, malignancy (concern DOAC vs warfarin). Initial parenteral anticoagulation (LMWH/UFH) bridge 5-7 days for warfarin; DOACs can start immediately. All effective; choice based on renal function, pregnancy status, bleeding risk.

metadata.topic: Anticoagulation Agents - LMWH vs UFH vs DOAC

text: Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist, slower onset (5-7 days), requires INR monitoring (goal 2-3 for VTE), multiple drug interactions, food interactions (vitamin K). Advantages: reversible (vitamin K, FFP), cheap long-term. Disadvantages: lots of monitoring, food/drug interactions. DOACs: faster onset, no monitoring, fewer interactions (apixaban/dabigatran least). Advantages: convenience, no monitoring. Disadvantages: not reversible (though reversal agents available), expensive initially, avoid if CrCl <15-30 depending on agent, not for cancer thrombosis. Choice: patient preference, renal function, drug interactions, ability to monitor (warfarin).

metadata.topic: Warfarin vs DOAC - Indications and Drug Interactions

text: IVC filter: mechanical barrier to prevent PE in anticoagulation contraindicated/failing patients. Indications: absolute = acute PE + anticoagulation contraindicated (active bleeding, HIT); relative = proximal DVT + high bleeding risk, unable to anticoagulate. Complications: filter thrombosis, IVC stenosis, migration, perforation (rare, usually benign), difficult retrieval if retrievable filter left in too long. Retrievable filters should be removed within 3 months (permanent filters reserved for expected lifelong contraindication). Anticoagulation should still be used when safe; filter is bridge only.

Post-thrombotic syndrome: chronic venous insufficiency (20-50% after DVT) presenting with leg swelling, pain, skin changes, ulceration. Risk: proximal DVT >distal, incomplete thrombus resolution, inadequate anticoagulation. Prevention: early anticoagulation, leg elevation, compression stockings (class 2-3, 30-40 mmHg for 2 years post-DVT shows benefit in some trials). Management: compression therapy, leg elevation, exercise, skin care, vein surgery if severe/ulceration. CEAP classification grades severity. No specific pharmacotherapy proven effective.

HAS-BLED score predicts major bleeding risk during anticoagulation: hypertension (1), abnormal renal/liver function (1 each), stroke (1), bleeding history (1), labile INR (1), elderly (>65, 1), drugs/alcohol (1 each). Score 0-1: low risk (<2% annual bleeding). 2-3: moderate risk. >3: high risk. VTE anticoagulation benefit usually outweighs bleeding risk; need shared decision-making in high-risk patients. Strategies to reduce bleeding: shorter initial anticoagulation, use DOAC if possible (more predictable than warfarin), PPI for GI bleed prevention if history, avoid NSAIDs.

metadata.topic: Bleeding Risk in VTE Anticoagulation - HAS-BLED Score

text: Warfarin reversal: vitamin K 10mg IV slow (onset 12-24h, persistent reversal), FFP 10-15 mL/kg (immediate but temporary, volume overload risk), prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC, 25 units/kg, preferred for urgent reversal). DOAC reversal: idarucizumab (dabigatran antidote), apixaban/rivaroxaban (activated factor X - andexanet alfa expensive/limited availability). Heparin reversal: protamine 1 mg per 100 units UFH (IV over 10 min, max 50 mg per dose). Reversal needs urgent evaluation by hematology if major bleeding.

metadata.topic: Reversal of Anticoagulation - Warfarin, DOAC, Heparin

text: Thrombophilia testing indicated: unprovoked VTE, VTE age <40, recurrent VTE, VTE with family history, mesenteric/portal venous thrombosis. Tests: Factor V Leiden (most common, 5% Caucasians), prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin deficiency, protein C/S deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome (anticardiolipin, beta-2 glycoprotein, lupus anticoagulant). Timing: test during anticoagulation (warfarin doesn't affect most), but avoid acute phase (elevated D-dimer, decreased protein S). Results guide extended anticoagulation decision if positive. Heterozygous Factor V Leiden = low recurrence risk; homozygous/multiple mutations = higher risk.

Cancer-associated VTE: 5-7% of cancer patients develop VTE; associated with poor outcomes. Historically warfarin preferred (DOACs not studied adequately in cancer trials). Recent trials (HOKUSAI-VTE-C, SELECT-D): DOAC (edoxaban, apixaban) non-inferior/superior to warfarin in cancer VTE. Practice evolving: DOACs now reasonable option for cancer VTE if not GI cancer or significant drug interactions. LMWH still reasonable if DOAC unavailable/contraindicated, or bridging. Duration: indefinite for active cancer; can discontinue after cancer remission (similar to non-cancer VTE). Inferior vena cava filter consideration if anticoagulation contraindicated.

metadata.topic: Cancer and VTE - DOAC vs Warfarin Controversy

text: Recurrent VTE: first episode treated 3 months, then evaluate for extended therapy. Second unprovoked VTE: indefinite anticoagulation usually recommended. Workup for recurrent despite anticoagulation: compliance check, efficacy of chosen agent (ensure therapeutic levels), occult malignancy (cancer screening if not recently done), thrombophilia, antiphospholipid syndrome, recurrent superficial thrombophlebitis. D-dimer guidance: persistently elevated post-anticoagulation = higher recurrence risk (favors extended anticoagulation). Extended anticoagulation (indefinite) reduces recurrence 80-85% vs stopping anticoagulation.

metadata.topic: Recurrent VTE - Workup and Prolonged Anticoagulation

text: PE Response Teams (PERT): multidisciplinary team (pulmonary, cardiology, interventional radiology, critical care, anticoagulation specialist) for risk stratification and management decisions in PE. Benefits: reduce time to intervention, improve risk stratification, increase thrombolysis use in appropriate candidates, reduce mortality (some studies). Available at larger medical centers. Useful for: massive PE, submassive with hemodynamic compromise, uncertainty about anticoagulation vs thrombolysis, complicated cases. Coordinated care improves outcomes vs isolated specialist recommendations.

VTE prophylaxis in hospitalized patients: anticoagulation (LMWH, fondaparinux, warfarin) or mechanical (compression devices, sequential compression stockings, early mobilization). Medical patients: risk assessment (Padua score, IMPROVE score); moderate-high risk = VTE prophylaxis. Surgical patients: type-specific prophylaxis (general surgery = LMWH 12 days; orthopedic = extended LMWH ±warfarin 10-35 days). Duration: continues until discharge or risk resolved. Contraindications: active bleeding, recent ICH, thrombocytopenia <50k, HIT. Mechanical prophylaxis alone if anticoagulation contraindicated.

metadata.topic: VTE Prophylaxis - Medical and Surgical Patients

text: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH): occurs if PE clots not completely resolved, leading to chronic RV strain, dyspnea, RV failure. Incidence 0.1-4% after acute PE. Risk: large PE, recurrent PE, inadequate anticoagulation. Diagnosis: right heart catheterization (elevated mean PA pressure >25 mmHg at rest), CT angiography (mosaic perfusion, webs/bands), ventilation-perfusion scan (mismatched defects). Management: lifelong anticoagulation, pulmonary vasodilators (ambrisentan, bosentan, sildenafil), pulmonary endarterectomy if operable (curative, 5-10 year survival benefit). Early recognition/referral critical.

metadata.topic: Pulmonary Hypertension Post-PE - Chronic Thromboembolic PH

text: CAP = pneumonia in non-hospitalized patient (or <48h after admission). Incidence 5-7 per 1000 adults/year. Mortality 1% outpatient, 5-7% hospitalized, 30-40% ICU. Most common: bacterial (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) vs viral (RSV, influenza, rhinovirus) vs atypical (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia).

CAP risk factors: age >65, smoking, alcohol, immunosuppression (HIV, steroids, biologics), diabetes, renal/liver disease, COPD, cardiovascular disease, recent viral illness. Initial assessment: vital signs (fever? tachycardia? tachypnea? hypoxia?), toxic appearance, comorbidities, functional status for outpatient vs inpatient decision.

metadata.topic: CAP - Risk Factors and Patient Assessment

text: CAP classic: cough (productive or dry), fever, dyspnea. Atypical presentations: elderly may lack fever, altered mental status instead; immunocompromised may be afebrile. Associated: pleuritic chest pain, rigors, malaise. Exam: fever, tachycardia, consolidation (tactile fremitus, dullness to percussion, egophony), crackles. Severity varies from mild outpatient to fulminant sepsis.

CXR: lobar consolidation (focal, dense), bronchopneumonia (patchy infiltrates), interstitial pattern (viral or atypical). Apical-posterior: TB, atypical (Legionella, Mycoplasma). Right lower lobe: most common. Pleural effusion suggests bacterial. Cavitation suggests anaerobes or TB. CXR lags symptoms by days; not required for diagnosis if clinical + sputum Gram stain/culture.

CBC: leukocytosis (>12k) typical, but absent in 10-15%; left shift common. CMP: renal function (creatinine), electrolytes (hyponatremia in severe/Legionella). BUN/Cr ratio elevated = dehydration. Blood cultures x2 before antibiotics if hospitalized (only 10% positive). Sputum Gram stain/culture if productive: identify organism, guide therapy. Lactate if severe/septic.

Viral pneumonia: bilateral diffuse infiltrates, interstitial pattern, elevated LDH. Bacterial: focal consolidation, pleural effusion more common. Atypical (Legionella, Mycoplasma): can mimic viral. Cold agglutinin positivity (>1:64) suggests Mycoplasma. Nasal swabs/rapid tests for influenza, RSV, COVID helpful. RT-PCR for specific pathogens. Treatment differs: viral = supportive + antivirals if indicated; bacterial = antibiotics.

Gram stain guides initial therapy: gram-positive cocci in pairs = Streptococcus pneumoniae (diplococcus). Gram-negative rods = H. influenzae, enteric gram-negatives. Gram-positive rods = anaerobes (if foul sputum/aspiration). Gram-negative coccobacillus = Legionella (but often Gram stain negative, requires special culture). Quality sputum: >25 PMNs, <10 epithelial cells per low power field. Poor quality: repeat or culture without interpretation.

Atypical pathogens: Legionella pneumophila, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Chlamydia psittaci (psittacosis = bird exposure), Coxiella burnetii (Q fever = farm exposure). Cannot be cultured routinely; require PCR, serology, or special culture. Presentation: constitutional symptoms, GI symptoms, diarrhea more common than typical CAP. Treatment: macrolides (azithromycin) or fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) cover atypicals.

CURB-65: Confusion (acute, new mental status change or disorientation), Urea >7 mmol/L (BUN >20 mg/dL), Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure (SBP <90 or DBP ≤60), age ≥65 years. Each = 1 point. Total 0-5 points. Predicts 30-day mortality. Risk stratification guides admission, ICU, and monitoring intensity. Simple, bedside tool requiring minimal labs/imaging.

CURB-65 score 0-1: outpatient management, low mortality (0-2%). Score 2: consider admission/closer monitoring, mortality 2-3%. Score 3: admission recommended, mortality 13-18%. Score 4-5: ICU/high-acuity care, mortality 40-50%. Negative predictive value >95% for low scores (0-1): safe to discharge if outpatient appropriate. Use with clinical judgment: comorbidities, ability to take oral medications, follow-up access.

CURB-65 works in ED/hospital settings to risk-stratify. Example: 75-year-old with RR=28, SBP=110, BUN=18, no confusion = 2 points (age + RR) = consider admission. Use alongside PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) if needed for low-risk confirmation. Limited in immunocompromised, atypical presentations. Not a substitute for clinical judgment.

Confusion = new acute change in mental status, NOT baseline dementia. Assessed via AMTS (Abbreviated Mental Test Score): age, time, place, person x2. Score 0 = alert/oriented; score ≥1 = confusion (1 point in CURB-65). In elderly baseline confusion, use informant history for acute change. Delirium superimposed on dementia still counts if acute worsening.

CURB-65 limitations: doesn't incorporate oxygen levels, doesn't assess sepsis/lactate severity, misses some ICU-bound patients. PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) more complex but slightly more sensitive for ICU risk. qSOFA (quick SOFA) for sepsis/septic shock: altered mental status + SBP ≤100 + RR ≥22. SOFA for ICU patients. Use CURB-65 as screening; clinical judgment trumps score.

Most common bacterial CAP pathogen (~40% of cases). Gram-positive diplococcus. Presents with acute onset fever, productive cough, rigors. Lobar consolidation typical. Blood cultures positive in 25-50% if not pre-treated. Complications: sepsis, meningitis (esp. if petechial rash), endocarditis (if prosthetic valve). Antibiotic resistance increasing (penicillin-resistant strains). Vaccination (PCV13, PPSV23) reduces incidence.

Gram-negative coccobacillus. Second most common. More common in COPD patients. Presentation similar to pneumococcus. X-ray: often bilateral, bronchopneumonia pattern. Ampicillin resistance common (30-50% in some regions) via beta-lactamase production. Complications: meningitis (type b, now rare with Hib vaccine), epiglottitis. Hib vaccine routine in childhood, but adult protection wanes.

Gram-negative diplococcus. Common in elderly and COPD. Usually lower lobe involvement. Typically mild-moderate disease, community outpatient pneumonia. Produces beta-lactamase; ampicillin/amoxicillin resistance ~80%. Susceptible to fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors. Less likely to cause bacteremia or invasive disease vs pneumococcus.

Aspiration pneumonia: from oral anaerobes after aspiration (risk: altered mental status, dysphagia, seizures, alcohol abuse). Pathogens: Peptostreptococcus, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides (all anaerobes). Presents subacutely (1-2 weeks), often with foul-smelling sputum/breath. Apical-posterior/superior segment infiltrate (gravity-dependent). Cavitation if delayed treatment. Penicillin V (not G) or clindamycin cover anaerobes.

Gram-negative enterics (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter) cause CAP in specific settings: healthcare-associated, severe COPD, recent antibiotics, ICU care. Klebsiella: associated with alcoholism, diabetes, chronic illness; can cavitate (aggressive). Pseudomonas aeruginosa: if COPD with FEV <25%, immunocompromised, recent hospitalizations. Require empiric coverage with fluoroquinolone or cephalosporin if risk factors present.

Outpatient CAP (CURB-65 0-1, low risk): first-line = amoxicillin 500mg TID x5 days (covers pneumococcus/H. flu) OR azithromycin 500mg day1, 250mg daily x4 days (covers atypicals too). Alternative if beta-lactam allergy: fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg daily x5, or moxifloxacin 400mg daily x5) covers both typical and atypical. Doxycycline (tetracycline, 100mg BID) also covers atypicals; avoid in pregnancy. Duration: 5-7 days typical.

Hospitalized CAP (CURB-65 2-3, moderate-severe): beta-lactam (amoxicillin-clavulanate, ceftriaxone, or cefpodoxime) + macrolide (azithromycin) OR fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) monotherapy. Fluoroquinolone monotherapy reasonable if patient cannot take IV. Beta-lactam + macrolide preferred if pneumococcus suspected and fluoroquinolone resistance risk low. Switching from IV to PO once clinically stable (defervescence, improved oxygenation).

metadata.topic: CAP - Empiric Antibiotic Therapy - Inpatient Non-ICU

text: Severe CAP in ICU (CURB-65 4-5, respiratory failure, shock): beta-lactam (ceftriaxone 1-2g IV q12h, or piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h) + fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily) OR + macrolide (azithromycin 500mg IV daily). Broad coverage for atypicals and resistant organisms. If Pseudomonas risk (severe COPD FEV <25%, recent antibiotics), use antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime) + fluoroquinolone.

Historical debate: fluoroquinolone monotherapy vs beta-lactam + macrolide. Meta-analyses show no mortality difference when used appropriately. Fluoroquinolone advantages: PO/IV formulations, atypical coverage, better lung penetration, no need for combination. Disadvantages: resistance emerging, Clostridium difficile risk, tendon rupture, QT prolongation. Beta-lactam + macrolide: proven, good outcomes, but more pills/side effects. Practice varies; both reasonable if age-appropriate and allergy status considered.

Azithromycin 500mg day1, then 250mg daily (Z-pack): covers pneumococcus, H. flu, Moraxella, atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia). GI side effects common (nausea, diarrhea). QT prolongation risk if given with other QT drugs. Erythromycin: older, more GI upset, less often used. Clarithromycin: similar coverage to azithromycin but also metabolizes via CYP3A4 (more drug interactions). Macrolides should not be used alone for CAP in elderly/comorbid (higher failure rates); use with beta-lactam.

metadata.topic: CAP - Macrolide Choice: Azithromycin vs Others

text: CAP antibiotic duration: typically 5-7 days total (shorter than historical 10-14 days). Shorter duration (3-5 days) safe if clinically stable, defervescent, able to take PO, adequate follow-up. Avoid prolonged course unless complications (empyema, metastatic infection). Switch to PO once tolerating, clinically improving (within 2-3 days typical). Outpatient: 5-7 days oral. Hospitalized: IV x 2-3 days, then PO x remaining days. Total course = OUTPATIENT duration (5 days) + any IV overlap.

De-escalation: start broad (empiric), then narrow based on culture/susceptibilities. Example: start ceftriaxone + azithromycin, culture identifies pneumococcus susceptible to penicillin, de-escalate to amoxicillin. Reduces antibiotic exposure, resistance, Clostridioides difficile risk. Monotherapy preferred when possible (e.g., fluoroquinolone monotherapy for CAP in compliant outpatient). Avoid prolonged broad-spectrum therapy. Stop when clinically improved (don't treat until negative cultures).

Legionella: gram-negative rod, found in water (air conditioning, cooling towers, hot tubs). Risk: age >50, smoking, immunocompromise, chronic lung disease. Mortality 1-5% with treatment, 25% without. Outbreaks rare in developed countries (water treatment better). Non-community source (travel, hotel stay) increases suspicion. Incubation: 2-10 days (longer than typical CAP).

metadata.topic: Legionella pneumophila - Epidemiology and Risk Factors

text: Legionella pneumonia: severe, with prominent constitutional symptoms (malaise, myalgias, headache), fever, GI symptoms (diarrhea, nausea), neurologic symptoms (confusion, lethargy). CXR: often bilateral infiltrates, can cavitate in severe cases. Hyponatremia common (SIADH). Labs: elevated transaminases, elevated LDH. Diagnosis: urine antigen test (rapid, not culture), sputum/BAL culture on special media (BMPA, CYE agar), serology (antibodies). Gram stain negative (poorly stains).

Legionella treatment: fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO daily x 7-10 days) or macrolide (azithromycin 500mg IV daily x 3-5 days, then PO x remaining). Fluoroquinolone preferred (better lung penetration, proven outcomes). Beta-lactams ineffective (not PBP-dependent). Duration: usually 7-10 days for hospitalized patients. ICU support if respiratory failure. Antibiotics should not be delayed waiting for definitive diagnosis if Legionella suspected clinically.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae: atypical bacterium (no cell wall), community-acquired, endemic (seasonal peaks fall/winter). Most common cause of atypical pneumonia. Spreads via respiratory droplets. Incubation 1-3 weeks (longer than bacterial CAP). Often affects young adults and children. Epidemics every 4-7 years. Can be mild self-limited disease to moderate pneumonia. Complications: myositis, myocarditis, neurologic (Guillain-Barré, encephalitis), hemolysis, cold agglutinin disease.

Mycoplasma: subacute onset (cough starts dry, may become productive), fever low-grade, systemic symptoms (headache, myalgias, malaise). CXR: interstitial infiltrates, often patchy, bilateral (can look like viral). Normal WBC or mild leukocytosis. Diagnosis: culture difficult/slow (requires special media, 2-3 weeks); serology (fourfold rise in acute/convalescent antibodies), cold agglutinin (>1:64 suggestive), PCR/serology testing (varies by lab). Gram stain negative (no cell wall).

Mycoplasma treatment: macrolide (azithromycin preferred) or fluoroquinolone or doxycycline (100mg BID x 7-14 days). Mild disease often self-limited; treat to shorten duration and prevent complications. Beta-lactams ineffective (no cell wall target). Duration: 7-10 days typical. Neurologic complications (Guillain-Barré, meningoencephalitis): more supportive care needed, steroids in some cases. Cold agglutinin disease (hemolysis): manage transfusions carefully (warm patient, avoid cold exposure). Myocarditis: monitor troponin, ECG, echo if symptomatic.

HAP = pneumonia occurring ≥48 hours after hospital admission in non-intubated patient. VAP (ventilator-associated pneumonia) = pneumonia in mechanically ventilated patient (typically ≥48h after intubation, sometimes <48h included if predisposed). HCAP (healthcare-associated CAP) = pneumonia in non-hospitalized but exposed to healthcare (nursing home, dialysis, chemotherapy, prolonged antibiotics, family member with resistant organism). All have higher mortality (15-20% for HAP, 25-50% for VAP) than CAP due to resistant organisms.

HAP/VAP organisms: multidrug-resistant gram-negatives (Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, extended-spectrum beta-lactamase [ESBL] Enterobacteriaceae), methicillin-resistant Staph aureus (MRSA), anaerobes, fungi (Candida if prolonged hospitalization/antibiotics). Risk factors for resistant organisms: prior antibiotics, prolonged hospitalization, ICU stay, mechanical ventilation, underlying disease severity. 50-80% of VAP due to gram-negative rods. Cultures (sputum, BAL, protected brush) guide therapy.

VAP suspected when: fever, leukocytosis, increased sputum production, worsening oxygenation, new infiltrate on CXR (though infiltrates common in ICU, etiology often unclear). Clinical VAP diagnosis imprecise (sensitivity only 60-80%, specificity 60-70%). Quantitative cultures (BAL >10^4 CFU/mL, PSB >10^3 CFU/mL) more specific but invasive. Routine sputum cultures poor discriminator (colonization vs infection). Procalcitonin elevation supports bacterial etiology. Consider non-infectious causes (aspiration, pulmonary edema, ARDS, atelectasis, PE).

VAP prevention bundle: head-of-bed elevation ≥30 degrees, oral care with chlorhexidine, spontaneous breathing trial daily (assess extubation readiness), DVT prophylaxis, stress ulcer prophylaxis, avoid gastric distension, subglottic secretion drainage (special tubes), early ambulation/mobilization. Selective decontamination of digestive tract (SDD) with antibiotics controversial (reduces VAP but may increase resistance). Bundle approach reduces VAP incidence by 30-50%.

HAP/VAP empiric therapy (pending cultures): broad coverage needed for resistant gram-negatives. Typical regimen: antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5g IV q6h, cefepime 1-2g IV q12h, meropenem 1g IV q8h) + fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750mg IV daily) OR aminoglycoside (amikacin, tobramycin; dosed once daily, levels monitored). Add vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q8-12h, trough 15-20) if MRSA risk or beta-lactam allergy.

VAP management: empiric broad therapy, then de-escalate based on cultures/sensitivities within 48-72 hours. Duration: 7-8 days for VAP (non-fermenting gram-negatives like Pseudomonas may benefit from longer courses if slow improvement). HAP: 7 days typical. Document clinical improvement before stopping: resolution of fever, decreasing sputum, improving oxygenation, stabilizing WBC. Longer therapy (14+ days) associated with increased resistance, Clostridioides difficile, candidiasis without mortality benefit.

VAP management includes aggressive weaning/extubation: daily spontaneous breathing trials (pressure support 7-8 cmH2O, PEEP 5, T-piece trials), assess readiness criteria (adequate oxygenation FiO2 ≤0.40-0.50, PEEP ≤5-8, respiratory rate <35, negative inspiratory force <-20, no sedation). Delay in weaning increases VAP risk, morbidity, mortality. Minimize sedation (daily sedation interruption), mobilization as tolerated. Reintubation risk 10-20%; assess swallow, mental status before extubation.

CAP can progress to sepsis (infection + SIRS: fever/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis/leukopenia) and septic shock (hypotension requiring vasopressors, end-organ dysfunction, lactate >2). Mortality 20-40% with sepsis, 40-60% with septic shock. Pneumococcal CAP particularly at risk. Management: early recognition, broad antibiotics (<1 hour), fluid resuscitation (30 mL/kg crystalloid), vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line), lactate clearance, source control (consider drainage if indicated).

metadata.topic: CAP Complications - Sepsis and Septic Shock

text: Empyema = pus in pleural space (bacterial pneumonia with effusion). Incidence 5-10% of hospitalized CAP. Presents with prolonged fever despite antibiotics, pleuritic pain, dyspnea. Diagnosis: pleural fluid with pH <7.0, glucose <60, LDH >1000, positive culture, or Gram stain positive. Requires drainage: chest tube/pigtail catheter, or VATS (video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) if loculated/thick. Antibiotics alone insufficient. Complications: failure to drain = bronchopleural fistula, septic shock, chronic drainage.

ARDS = bilateral infiltrates, PaO2/FiO2 ratio <300, no evidence of hydrostatic pulmonary edema. Pneumonia (bacterial and viral) is leading cause of ARDS. Pathophysiology: increased capillary permeability, alveolar inflammation, surfactant dysfunction. Mortality 25-50% depending on severity. Management: lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volumes 6-8 mL/kg, permissive hypercapnia, PEEP optimization), proning if severe, fluid restriction after initial resuscitation. Prone positioning reduces mortality if P/F ratio <100 and early treatment.

metadata.topic: CAP Complications - Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS)

text: Spontaneous pneumothorax can occur with bacterial pneumonia (especially staphylococcal, pneumococcal, pneumatosis formation). Presents with acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, hypoxia. Diagnosis: CXR or CT shows collapsed lung, pleural line. Small <2cm at hilum, asymptomatic: observation + supplemental oxygen. Moderate-large or symptomatic: chest tube (pigtail catheter often preferred). Persistent air leak: evaluate for bronchopleural fistula (high-resolution CT). VATS if recurrent or persistent.

Parapneumonic effusion = pleural fluid with bacterial CAP but sterile (not empyema). Incidence 20-40% of hospitalized CAP. Fluid characteristics: pH 7.0-7.20, glucose >60, LDH variable, negative cultures. Uncomplicated effusions: usually resolve with antibiotic therapy, no drainage needed. Complicated: pH <7.0, glucose <60, high LDH (risk of progression to empyema); consider drainage if recurrent fevers despite antibiotics. Serial ultrasound/CT to monitor evolution.

Hematogenous spread from pneumonia can cause: meningitis (especially pneumococcal, 5-10% of bacteremia), endocarditis (especially if prosthetic valve, IVDU, Group A Streptococcus), septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, brain abscess, splenic/renal infarcts. Signs: persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics, new cardiac murmur, neck stiffness, focal neurologic deficits. Diagnosis: blood cultures (already drawn), CSF if meningitis suspected, echo if endocarditis, MRI if abscess. Management: longer antibiotic courses (2-4 weeks), imaging, sometimes surgical intervention.

Viral pneumonia (influenza, parainfluenza, COVID-19, myocarditis viruses) can cause myocarditis/pericarditis. Bacterial pneumonia less common but can cause postpericardial/post-pneumonic state. Myocarditis: elevated troponin, decreased ejection fraction on echo, arrhythmias, cardiogenic shock. Pericarditis: pleuritic chest pain, friction rub, ECG PR depression, tamponade risk. Management: cardiac monitoring, troponin/BNP, echo, supportive care. Pericardiocentesis if tamponade. Steroids sometimes considered for viral myocarditis (controversial).

Lung abscess = localized collection of pus (necrotic lung tissue) due to pneumonia. Risk: aspiration, anaerobic organisms, poor dentition, alcoholism, immunosuppression. Presents with persistent fever, productive cough (sometimes foul-smelling), weight loss. CXR: cavitary lesion with air-fluid level (classic). Diagnosis: CT chest confirms abscess. Cultures: sputum, BAL (anaerobes need special handling). Treatment: prolonged antibiotics (anaerobic coverage: penicillin V + clindamycin, or amoxicillin-clavulanate, or piperacillin-tazobactam), x 2-4 weeks. Percutaneous drainage if large (>4-5cm), non-responsive to antibiotics. Rarely surgical resection.

PCP: fungal infection (formerly Pneumocystis carinii). Risk: CD4 <200 cells/μL (AIDS), solid organ transplant, prolonged corticosteroids (>20mg prednisone x >1 month), certain immunosuppressants (TNF-alpha inhibitors, JAK inhibitors). Presentation: subacute (1-4 weeks) dyspnea, dry cough, fever, chest pain. Exam: tachypnea, hypoxia, normal lung sounds initially (later crackles). CXR: bilateral interstitial infiltrates, can be normal early (15-20% of cases). ABG shows hypoxia with large A-a gradient.

metadata.topic: PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia) - Risk Factors and Presentation

text: PCP diagnosis: induced sputum (cough induction with hypertonic saline), BAL with DFA stain (polychrome methylene silver or immunofluorescence), PCR testing (most sensitive). Chest imaging: CXR may be normal; CT shows ground-glass opacities. Treatment: TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) 15mg/kg TMP IV/PO q6h x 14-21 days (first-line). Alternatives: pentamidine, clindamycin + primaquine, atovaquone. Steroids added if PaO2 <70 or A-a gradient >35 (reduces mortality). Prophylaxis: TMP-SMX daily if CD4 <200 (can discontinue if CD4 >200 x 3 months on ART).

Pneumonia in HIV varies by CD4 count: CD4 >200: bacterial CAP similar to immunocompetent. CD4 100-200: PCP, Cryptococcus, TB coinfection increased. CD4 <50: CMV, Mycobacterium avium (MAC), fungal (Histoplasma, Coccidioides). Diagnosis approach: CXR, sputum culture, consider PCR for common organisms, bronchoscopy if CD4 <100 or atypical presentation. Empiric therapy depends on CD4; include TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolone if CD4 <200. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) critical to immune reconstitution; must be managed carefully with IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome).

metadata.topic: CAP in HIV/AIDS - Approach and Opportunistic Infections

text: CMV pneumonitis: risk if CD4 <50 or other severe immunosuppression (transplant, high-dose steroids). Presents with dyspnea, hypoxia (often severe, hypoxemia disproportionate to infiltrate), low-grade fever. CXR: diffuse interstitial infiltrates, can appear normal. Diagnosis: CMV PCR blood (high viral load suggests disease), BAL with CMV culture or PCR, histology (inclusion bodies). Difficult to diagnose; high suspicion needed. Treatment: ganciclovir or valganciclovir for 2+ weeks. Cidofovir if ganciclovir-resistant. Mortality high (40-90%) if untreated.

Opportunistic infection prophylaxis guided by CD4 count: CD4 <200: TMP-SMX (covers PCP, Toxoplasma, some bacteria). CD4 <100: also consider azithromycin (MAC prophylaxis). CD4 <50: also ganciclovir or valganciclovir (CMV). Non-HIV immunocompromised (transplant, TNF inhibitors): TB prophylaxis if LTBI, fungal prophylaxis per risk. Vaccination crucial: PCV13/PPSV23 (if CD4 >200), influenza annual, COVID-19. ART initiation (CD4 <50 recommended urgent). Monitor CD4 recovery on ART; prophylaxis often discontinued when CD4 >200-250 x 3 months.

Core principles: (1) optimize empiric therapy (narrow when culture results available), (2) avoid unnecessarily broad agents (fluoroquinolones only when indicated, avoid double coverage), (3) shorten duration (5-7 days CAP, 7-8 days VAP, not 10-14 days), (4) switch IV to PO early (oral bioavailability good for many agents), (5) avoid combination therapy unless needed (monotherapy when possible), (6) use local antibiograms to guide empiric choices. Goal: reduce C. difficile, resistance, side effects, costs while maintaining clinical outcomes.

metadata.topic: Antibiotic Stewardship - Core Principles in Pneumonia

text: De-escalation strategy: (1) start broad empiric therapy based on risk factors, (2) obtain cultures before antibiotics if possible, (3) reassess at 48-72 hours with culture results, (4) narrow therapy to cover identified pathogen(s), (5) discontinue redundant agents, (6) switch broad agents to narrow ones (fluoroquinolone to amoxicillin if susceptible pneumococcus). Example: start piperacillin-tazobactam for VAP, culture shows H. influenzae susceptible to ceftriaxone, de-escalate to ceftriaxone monotherapy. Improves outcomes by reducing toxicity, cost, resistance.

metadata.topic: De-escalation - From Broad to Narrow Therapy

text: Monotherapy preferred when possible (fewer pills, fewer side effects, lower cost). Fluoroquinolone monotherapy adequate for outpatient CAP (covers typical + atypical). Combination (beta-lactam + macrolide) justified if: severe CAP, ICU admission, shock, need atypical coverage, or local resistance patterns suggest combination benefit. VAP often requires combination (broad gram-negative coverage + MRSA if risk). De-escalate to monotherapy once culture shows susceptible pathogen. Avoid unnecessary dual therapy (e.g., two beta-lactams) unless specific indication (inadequate coverage, resistance).

Clinical stability (can discontinue or step-down antibiotics when): (1) defervescence ≥24-48 hours, (2) no acute respiratory distress, (3) improved oxygenation, (4) oral intake adequate, (5) WBC normalizing, (6) lactate normalized, (7) hemodynamically stable without vasopressors. Don't wait for: complete CXR clearance (lags clinical improvement), negative follow-up cultures (no benefit), or arbitrary day-5/7. Earlier recognition of stability allows IV-to-PO switch, shorter course, discharge. Premature discontinuation risks relapse; clinical judgment needed.

metadata.topic: Clinical Stability Criteria and Antibiotic Discontinuation

text: Fluoroquinolone appropriate: outpatient CAP (monotherapy, no IV access), COPD with risk factors, atypical pneumonia (Legionella, Mycoplasma), mixed infection (beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone, then de-escalate), PCN allergy, GI intolerance to beta-lactams. Inappropriate: routine mild CAP in young patient (amoxicillin sufficient), empiric HAP/VAP if low MRSA/Pseudomonas risk (narrower agent better), prophylaxis (resistance risk). Side effects: Clostridioides difficile, QT prolongation, tendon rupture, neuropathy. Cost higher than beta-lactams. Reserve for indication-driven use. Resistance emerging (especially Pseudomonas).

Switch IV to PO (oral step-down) when: patient tolerating oral intake, able to absorb medications (no vomiting), adequate oral bioavailability of chosen agent, clinical improvement trend. Agents with good oral bioavailability: fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin 750mg PO = IV equivalent), macrolides (azithromycin), doxycycline, amoxicillin/clavulanate. Switch timing: 2-3 days into IV therapy once clinically improving. Benefits: reduced cost, line removal, early discharge, less nosocomial infection risk. Don't delay oral step-down in stable patients; shortens hospitalization without compromising outcomes.

metadata.topic: IV-to-PO Transition and Oral Antibiotic Bioavailability

text: AKI (acute kidney injury): abrupt decline in renal function. KDIGO criteria: ≥1.5× increase in creatinine within 7 days OR urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6-12 hours. Stage 1: 1.5-1.9× Cr, output <0.5 mL/kg/hr x 6-8h. Stage 2: 2.0-2.9× Cr, output <0.5 mL/kg/hr x 16h. Stage 3: ≥3× Cr or Cr ≥4 or initiation RRT, output <0.3 mL/kg/hr x 24h. Mortality increases with AKI stage: 2-5% Stage 1, 5-10% Stage 2, 15-25% Stage 3. Risk factors: age, CKD, diabetes, hypotension, nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARBs in certain settings, aminoglycosides, contrast).

metadata.topic: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) - KDIGO Definition and Staging

text: Prerenal AKI: hypoperfusion to kidneys (hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, renal artery stenosis). Incidence 55-70% of AKI. Pathophysiology: reduced glomerular filtration pressure -> oliguria, preserved tubular function. Diagnosis: FeNa <1% (fractional excretion sodium), urine osmolality >500, BUN/Cr ratio >20, urine sodium <20. Response to fluids rapidly (if prerenal). Risk: progression to ATN if prolonged hypoperfusion. Management: address underlying cause (restore volume, increase cardiac output, relieve obstruction), avoid nephrotoxins, avoid excessive fluids (risk pulmonary edema if cardiogenic shock).

Intrinsic AKI (25-30% of AKI): direct kidney injury. ATN (most common intrinsic AKI): tubular epithelial cell necrosis. Causes: hypotension/ischemia (ischemic ATN) or nephrotoxins (toxic ATN). Ischemic ATN: sepsis, cardiogenic shock, major surgery, rhabdomyolysis. Toxic ATN: aminoglycosides, cisplatin, myoglobin (rhabdo), hemoglobin (massive hemolysis), contrast (volume depletion risk), NSAIDs, ACE-I (in certain volume-depleted states). Diagnosis: FeNa >2%, muddy brown casts (myoglobin-stained), urine sodium >40. Recovery 7-21 days typically (tubule regeneration). Management: supportive (fluids, avoid further nephrotoxins), RRT if oliguria/electrolyte dysregulation. Oliguric ATN worse prognosis (mortality 50-60%) than non-oliguric (mortality 5-10%).

Postrenal AKI (5-10% of AKI): urinary tract obstruction distal to kidney. Causes: kidney stones, tumors, strictures, neurogenic bladder (spinal cord injury, cauda equina), BPH prostate obstruction, retroperitoneal fibrosis. Unilateral obstruction may not cause AKI (contralateral kidney compensates); bilateral obstruction required. Presentation: anuria (absent urine), flank pain (stones), suprapubic distension (bladder obstruction). Diagnosis: ultrasound (hydronephrosis), CT (stone, tumor), post-void residual volume (elevated in bladder obstruction). Management: catheterization (Foley or suprapubic) for bladder outlet obstruction, urology consultation for upper tract obstruction (stent, percutaneous nephrostomy). Outcomes: excellent if relief <1 week; delayed relief risk permanent renal dysfunction (tubular atrophy if prolonged).

Muddy brown casts: pathognomonic for ATN (myoglobin-stained tubular cells + Tamm-Horsfall protein), appear in ischemic/toxic ATN. RBC casts: indicate glomerulonephritis (RPGN/IGAN/PSGN/lupus). WBC casts: interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis. Hyaline casts: benign, concentrated urine. Crystals: calcium oxalate (star/dumbbell-shaped) = ethylene glycol toxicity, uric acid (diamond/rhomboid) = hyperuricemia/tumor lysis, urea nitrogen, sulfur (sulfadiazine crystals). Crystal-induced AKI requires aggressive fluids (urine output >200 mL/hr), urine alkalinization (some crystals), specific antidotes (fomepizole for ethylene glycol). Absence of casts doesn't exclude intrinsic AKI (10% have granular/epithelial cells only).

metadata.topic: Urinalysis Interpretation in AKI - Casts and Crystals

text: Rhabdomyolysis: skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin (brown protein) into urine. Causes: crush injury, statins (rare but serious), alcohol, seizures, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia. Presentation: brown/cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), muscle pain, hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, hyperuricemia. AKI mechanism: myoglobin tubular precipitation, direct tubular toxicity. Risk factors for AKI in rhabdo: volume depletion, acidic urine (myoglobin precipitates better at low pH). Management: aggressive IV hydration (goal urine output 200-300 mL/hr, maintain intravascular volume), urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (pH >6.5), avoid NSAIDs/ACE-I (worsen volume depletion). Monitor CK (peaks day 3), electrolytes (hyperkalemia), calcium (treat symptomatic hypocalcemia cautiously, risk metastatic calcification). RRT if oliguria/severe electrolyte dysregulation.

metadata.topic: Rhabdomyolysis and Myoglobinuria - AKI from Muscle Breakdown

text: NSAIDs: inhibit prostaglandin synthesis, reduce renal blood flow. Risk in volume-depleted states (heart failure, sepsis, cirrhosis), elderly, pre-existing CKD. ACE-I/ARBs: block angiotensin II (efferent arteriole vasoconstriction). Beneficial in proteinuric disease but harmful in volume depletion (loss of efferent arteriole tone = reduced GFR). Hold ACE-I/ARBs if: SBP <90, acute diarrhea/vomiting, acute AKI, renal artery stenosis. Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin): concentrate in proximal tubule, dose-dependent & concentration-dependent nephrotoxicity. Risk: prolonged therapy, high trough levels, volume depletion, baseline CKD. Use extended-interval dosing (once-daily amikacin 15 mg/kg) reduces nephrotoxicity vs q8h dosing. Monitor: Cr, drug levels, BUN. Alternatives: fluoroquinolones if susceptible organism.

Contrast-induced nephropathy: AKI within 48-72h of iodinated contrast exposure. Risk: baseline CKD (GFR <60), diabetes, volume depletion, age >75, heart failure, multiple contrast exposures. Mechanism: direct tubular toxicity, osmotic injury, renal vasoconstriction. Prevention: IV hydration (0.9% NS 1 mL/kg/hr x 4-6 hours before + 6 hours after contrast; 3 mL/kg if LVEF <35), metformin hold 48h post-contrast (accumulation if AKI develops), aminoglycosides hold (additive nephrotoxicity). N-acetylcysteine controversial (prior evidence, later trials negative). Sodium bicarbonate vs isotonic saline: saline preferred (randomized trials show no superiority of bicarbonate). Management: monitor Cr at 48-72h, adjust medications if AKI develops.

CRRT (continuous renal replacement therapy): low blood flow (150-200 mL/min), gradual fluid/solute removal. Advantages: hemodynamic stability in hypotensive patients, better metabolic control, allows nutrition. Disadvantages: immobilizes patient (ICU-bound), anticoagulation needs, expensive, staffing intensive. Indications: hypotension, need rapid fluid removal (not compatible with intermittent), electrolyte dysregulation (needs frequent adjustment). Intermittent hemodialysis: high blood flow (300-500 mL/min), rapid removal. Advantages: shorter duration, mobilizes patient, less anticoagulation. Disadvantages: hemodynamic instability (hypotension, arrhythmias) post-dialysis, slower electrolyte correction (risk rebound), less suited for hypotensive patients. Choice depends: clinical stability, hemodynamics, ICU capacity. CRRT preferred in sepsis/shock (hemodynamic instability); intermittent reasonable in stable AKI.

metadata.topic: Renal Replacement Therapy (RRT) - CRRT vs Intermittent Hemodialysis

text: RRT indications (RIFLE/KDIGO based): (1) Refractory hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5 refractory to medical management). (2) Refractory pulmonary edema/fluid overload (oliguria, high fluid requirements). (3) Severe metabolic acidosis (pH <7.1 refractory). (4) Uremia symptoms (encephalopathy, pericarditis, bleeding). (5) Severe electrolyte abnormalities (hyponatremia, hypocalcemia unresponsive to treatment). Relative contraindications: hemodynamic instability (relative; CRRT preferred over intermittent), active bleeding (if anticoagulation for CRRT needed; heparin-free circuits possible), thrombocytopenia <50k (bleeding risk with anticoagulation). Early RRT (within 24-48h of AKI diagnosis) may improve outcomes in severe AKI (KDIGO 3) based on recent trials; avoid delay if indications present.

metadata.topic: RRT Indications - When to Start and Relative Contraindications

text: Hyperkalemia: K+ >5.5 mEq/L. Symptoms: weakness, palpitations, syncope (rare until K+ >7). EKG changes (progressive): peaked T waves (K+ 5.5-6.5), prolonged PR/widened QRS (K+ 6.5-7.5), loss of P wave/bradycardia, sine wave (K+ >8, cardiac arrest imminent). Absent symptoms/EKG doesn't exclude danger (can progress rapidly). Management algorithm: (1) Calcium gluconate 10-20 mL of 10% IV bolus (cardiac membrane stabilization, no K+ lowering, 30-60 min duration). (2) Insulin 10 units IV + dextrose 25g (50 mL D50W) = shift K+ intracellularly, effect 10-20 min, lasts 4-6 hours. (3) Beta-2 agonist (albuterol 10-20 mg nebulized) = K+ shift, slower onset. (4) Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 amps IV (raises pH, K+ shift), use if acidemia. (5) Diuretics (furosemide) if euvolemic. (6) RRT if refractory/oliguric. (7) Cation exchange resin (kayexalate, sodium polystyrene sulfonate) = slow K+ removal via GI excretion.

metadata.topic: Hyperkalemia - EKG Changes and Treatment Algorithm

text: Hyponatremia: Na+ <135 mEq/L. Classify by osmolality: hyperosmolar (hyperglycemia, mannitol, contrast), isosmolar (pseudohyponatremia from lipemia/proteinemia, now rare with direct Na+ measurement), hypoosmolar (true dilution). Hypoosmolar causes: SIADH (euvolemic, urine osmolality >100, urine Na+ >40), diuretics (hypovolemic, urine Na+ >20, low urine osmolality), heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic (hypervolemic). SIADH diagnosis: euvolemic hyponatremia, low serum osmolality (<280), high urine osmolality (>100), high urine Na+ (>40), normal renal/adrenal/thyroid function. Causes: CNS (meningitis, head trauma, seizures), pulmonary (infection, positive pressure ventilation), malignancy (lung cancer, SCLC), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, vincristine, MDMA), pain/stress.

Symptomatic hyponatremia: nausea, headache, confusion, lethargy, seizures (Na+ <120), coma, death (if severe <110). Acute hyponatremia (<48h): cells haven't adapted, increased intracellular fluid volume -> cerebral edema risk at lower Na+ levels. Chronic hyponatremia (>48h): osmolytes extruded from cells, cerebral edema less likely even if Na+ very low. Correction rate critical: too-rapid correction (>12 mEq/L in 24h) risks central pontine myelinolysis (demyelination, locked-in syndrome, death). Acute symptomatic: 3% hypertonic saline (NaCl 3%, 1 mL/kg IV bolus, repeat once if still seizing), aim for 4-6 mEq/L rise per hour. Chronic asymptomatic: fluid restriction (SIADH), slow correction 4-8 mEq/L per 24h.

metadata.topic: Symptomatic vs Asymptomatic Hyponatremia - Acute vs Chronic

text: 3% hypertonic saline (NaCl 3%): reserved for symptomatic acute hyponatremia. Dosing: 1-2 mL/kg IV bolus (50-100 mL), repeat once after seizure cessation, then reassess. Calculate Na+ rise: change in Na+ = ([Na+ infused] - [Na+ serum]) / (total body water + 1). Example: 100 mL 3% saline (513 mEq/L) in 70 kg patient (TBW ~42L) = ~1 mEq/L rise. Fluid restriction: first-line for SIADH, restrict to 500-800 mL/day. Vaptans (tolvaptan, conivaptan): vasopressin antagonists, aquaretics (promote free water excretion). Used in SIADH refractory to fluid restriction; oral or IV. Caution: rapid Na+ correction risk, expensive, hepatotoxicity monitoring needed. Monitor: serum Na+ q2-4h during acute treatment, avoid hypernatremia (over-correction), neuro checks.

metadata.topic: Hyponatremia Treatment - 3% Saline, Fluid Restriction, Vaptans

text: Hypernatremia: Na+ >145 mEq/L. Causes: insensible losses (diabetes insipidus, sweating, diarrhea, inadequate intake, hypertonic fluid administration. Diabetes insipidus (DI): central (pituitary damage/surgery, hypothyroidism, trauma, idiopathic) vs nephrogenic (congenital, lithium, hypercalcemia, CKD). Presentation: polyuria, polydipsia (if intact thirst), hypernatremia (if intake insufficient), hypertonicity symptoms (restlessness, confusion, lethargy). Free water deficit calculation: FWD (liters) = (0.6 × body weight kg × [(Na+ serum / 140) - 1]). Replacement: calculate rate to replace over 48 hours (slower than hyponatremia correction, risk cerebral edema). D5W or 0.45% NS. Treat underlying cause (vasopressin if central DI, NSAIDs/amiloride if nephrogenic DI).

metadata.topic: Hypernatremia - Causes and Free Water Deficit Calculation

text: Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS): central pontine + extrapontine myelinolysis from overly rapid Na+ correction (>12 mEq/L in 24h). Risk: chronic hyponatremia (cells adapted), rapid correction re-creates osmotic gradient = cellular dehydration -> demyelination. Symptoms: flaccid paralysis, locked-in appearance, death (acute), behavioral changes/movement disorders (delayed recovery phase). Prevention: limit correction to 4-8 mEq/L per 24h (chronic) or 10-12 mEq/L per 24h (acute symptomatic). Monitor: serum Na+ q4-6h during acute correction, adjust infusion rate. If Na+ rising too fast: stop hypertonic saline, reduce rate, use dextrose (free water) to slow correction. Treat underlying disorder (SIADH = fluid restriction, DI = vasopressin). ODS irreversible; prevention critical.

metadata.topic: Correction Rate Calculations - Avoiding Osmotic Demyelination

text: TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone): pituitary hormone stimulating thyroid hormone production. Feedback: low T4 -> high TSH (stimulates production); high T4 -> low TSH (suppresses). T4 (thyroxine): inactive precursor, 99% protein-bound, half-life 7 days. T3 (triiodothyronine): active hormone, faster-acting, converted from T4 peripherally. Reverse T3: inactive metabolite, increased in illness/stress. Free T4/T3: unbound, biologically active (preferred to measure). TSH most sensitive screening test for dysfunction. Normal TSH 0.4-4 mIU/L; reference ranges vary by lab.

metadata.topic: Thyroid Physiology - TSH, T3, T4, Reverse T3

text: TSH advantages: most sensitive for primary hypo/hyperthyroidism, inexpensive, standard screening. First-line test for suspected thyroid disease. Limitations: (1) central hypo/hyperthyroidism (pituitary/hypothalamus disease) = normal TSH despite abnormal free T4 (rare). (2) Acute illness suppresses TSH (euthyroid sick syndrome). (3) Pregnancy, medications (estrogens, dopamine agonists, amiodarone) affect interpretation. (4) Population variation: 10-15% outside standard range without disease. Recommendation: check free T4 if TSH abnormal to confirm clinical significance.

metadata.topic: TSH as Screening Test - Strengths and Limitations

text: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH, low free T4 (primary). Causes: Hashimoto thyroiditis (90% developed countries, autoimmune, anti-TPO/anti-thyroglobulin antibodies), iodine deficiency (worldwide leading cause of preventable hypothyroidism), medications (amiodarone, lithium, interferon), central causes (pituitary, hypothalamus). Hashimoto: slow progressive destruction, women >men, genetic predisposition. Iodine deficiency: endemic goiter, cretinism if severe in pregnancy. Presentation: fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia, constipation, myxedema (skin thickening/puffiness), depression. Diagnosis: elevated TSH, low free T4 (low TSH = central hypo).

Levothyroxine (synthetic T4): first-line treatment for hypothyroidism. Dosing: 1.6 mcg/kg daily (usually 25-200 mcg depending on baseline TSH/body weight). Start low (25-50 mcg), increase by 25-50 mcg every 4-6 weeks until euthyroid. Take on empty stomach (fasting absorption best, 30-60 min before food/supplements). Recheck TSH 6-8 weeks after dose change (steady state takes 4-6 weeks due to long half-life). Titrate to TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L (target patient-specific: lower in post-thyroidectomy/thyroid cancer, elderly prefer TSH 1-3). Monitor annually once stable.

metadata.topic: Hypothyroidism Treatment - Levothyroxine Dosing and Monitoring

text: Levothyroxine interactions: calcium (dairy, supplements), iron (ferrous sulfate), magnesium, aluminum hydroxide (antacids), proton pump inhibitors all decrease absorption (space dosing by 4+ hours). Estrogens (oral contraceptives, HRT) increase clearance; may need higher levothyroxine dose. Amiodarone, salicylates, anticonvulsants affect binding/metabolism. Switching brands: maintain same manufacturer if possible (bioequivalence varies slightly). Adequate dosing indicated by: TSH at goal, symptoms resolved (energy, weight stable, normal temperature), normal heart rate. Over-treatment risks: atrial fibrillation, osteoporosis, cardiac events (especially elderly/cardiac disease).

metadata.topic: Levothyroxine - Drug Interactions and Bioavailability Issues

text: Hyperthyroidism: low TSH, high free T4 (primary). Causes: Graves disease (autoimmune, 70% cases, TSI antibodies), toxic adenoma/multinodular goiter (10-15%), thyroiditis (viral, postpartum, drug-induced), drugs (iodine excess, amiodarone). Graves: women >men, genetic predisposition, associated ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos, diplopia), dermopathy (pretibial myxedema). Presentation: heat intolerance, anxiety, palpitations, weight loss, tremor, hyperdefecation, thyroid bruit (Graves), stare/lid lag. Diagnosis: low TSH, elevated free T4, elevated free T3 (often). TSI antibodies confirm Graves.

metadata.topic: Hyperthyroidism - Graves Disease and Toxic Nodule

text: Thyroid storm: decompensated hyperthyroidism, mortality 1-5% even treated, >25% if untreated. Triggers: inadequate antithyroid treatment, infection, surgery/anesthesia in untreated hyperthyroid. Presentation: fever (often high, >38.5C), tachycardia (often >140), atrial fibrillation, altered mental status, thyroid enlargement, GI symptoms (diarrhea, nausea), jaundice, hepatomegaly. Pathophysiology: excess thyroid hormone causing sympathomimetic toxicity, altered TH metabolism. Management: urgent hospitalization, beta-blockers (propranolol 40-80 mg q6h, reduces symptoms + T4->T3 conversion), PTU 150-200 mg q6h (preferred over methimazole in crisis for toxicity profile), Lugol's solution or SSKI 1-2 drops q6-8h (blocks T4 release, start after PTU 1 hour to prevent thyroid hormone synthesis worsening).

PTU (propylthiouracil): blocks thyroid peroxidase (TPO), reduces T4/T3 synthesis + inhibits T4->T3 conversion (faster symptom improvement). Dosing: 50-100 mg TID (start), taper to 25-50 mg TID maintenance. Risk: hepatotoxicity (0.1-0.3%, can be fulminant), agranulocytosis (rare), rash. Preferred in first trimester pregnancy (crosses placenta less), thyroid storm (faster T4->T3 inhibition). Methimazole: blocks TPO, T4/T3 synthesis only. Dosing: 5-20 mg daily. Risk: agranulocytosis (0.3%), rash, arthralgia. Preferred first-line (once-daily dosing, lower hepatotoxicity). Pregnancy: PTU first trimester, switch methimazole second/third trimester (PTU hepatotoxicity risk, methimazole embryopathy rare). Monitor: CBC baseline, LFTs baseline, repeat if fever/infection/jaundice.

metadata.topic: PTU vs Methimazole - Dosing and Toxicity Profile

text: Beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol, metoprolol): treat adrenergic symptoms (palpitations, tremor, anxiety) WITHOUT affecting thyroid hormone production. Used while waiting for PTU/methimazole or radioactive iodine to take effect (weeks). Propranolol preferred (also blocks T4->T3 conversion, reducing hormone activation). Dosing: propranolol 40-120 mg daily (TID-QID), target HR 60-80. Continue during antithyroid treatment until euthyroid (TSH normalized). Monitor: HR, symptoms, hypoglycemia risk (beta-blockers mask). Not sufficient monotherapy; must combine with PTU/methimazole or radioactive iodine for definitive treatment.

metadata.topic: Beta-Blockers for Symptom Control in Hyperthyroidism

text: Radioactive iodine (I-131): sodium iodide oral, accumulates in thyroid, destroys hyperactive tissue. Advantages: outpatient, definitive, single dose. Disadvantages: delayed effect (4-12 weeks to euthyroid), radiation exposure (low, contraindicated in pregnancy/breastfeeding), hypothyroidism develops in 80% over lifetime (requires levothyroxine replacement). Pregnancy/lactation absolute contraindication. Thyroidectomy: surgical ablation of thyroid. Advantages: immediate definitive cure, option if Graves ophthalmopathy (may worsen post-I131). Disadvantages: perioperative risk, laryngeal nerve injury (voice/breathing), hypoparathyroidism. Pretreated with PTU/methimazole + beta-blockers + iodine solution (Lugol's) x 7-10 days pre-op to reduce bleeding/thyroid storm risk.

metadata.topic: Radioactive Iodine and Thyroidectomy - Definitive Treatment Options

text: Thyroiditis: inflammation of thyroid gland, various etiologies. Viral (subacute): self-limited, follows viral URI, presents with thyroid pain, hyperthyroidism phase (T4 release) -> hypothyroid phase (recovery), 3-6 months course. Autoimmune (Hashimoto): progressive destruction (covered under hypothyroidism).
